items.title: feat(sglang): orchestrate warm TP1 crash failover
items.body:
Part 7 of 14 in #14704. Builds on #14711.

## Why

Fast recovery needs a preinitialized shadow, but it must not serve or write shared KV until the active engine is fenced.

## What changes

- Give the primary an exclusive failover lock before activation.
- Start and pause a warm TP1 shadow outside discovery.
- Promote the shadow only after it acquires the released lock.
- Monitor child processes and bound discovery unregister/register work.
- Reuse the persistent allocation and content directory during promotion.

This supports crash failover. Cooperative ownership handoff is intentionally unsupported.

## Validation

The cumulative TP1 launcher-only crash E2E produces exact output, adopts six HBM pages, reuses 384 cached prompt tokens, and leaks no persistent allocation.

Next: #14713 strengthens writer fencing.

## Summary

Day-0 Dynamo recipes for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SGLang. Each target uses 8x GB200 GPUs.

| Target | Shape | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `sglang/agg-gb200` | 2 workers, TP4 and EP4 each | KV-aware routing, DSpark speculative decoding |
| `sglang/disagg-gb200` | 1 prefill + 1 decode, TP4 each | Mooncake KV transfer over the NVLink fabric |

The checkpoint is FP8 dense with FP4 MoE experts. The KV cache is FP8. Both targets serve up to 1,048,576 tokens of context, and both use the `deepseek_v41` reasoning and tool-call parsers.

The disaggregated target carries no speculative decoding. SGLang refuses DSpark under prefill and decode disaggregation for this model, and the guard is DeepSeek-V4 specific:

```
ValueError: DeepSeek-V4.1 does not support PD disaggregation with
speculative decoding yet; disable it to serve this model.
```

Each worker needs TP4 and a GB200 node holds 4 GPUs. So prefill and decode always sit on different nodes, and KV crosses nodes. The generic target pins Mooncake to TCP with `MC_FORCE_TCP=1`; the `gke-rdma` target drops that pin and uses RDMA. Neither takes the NVLink fabric. The fabric is faster, but it needs both workers in one NVLink clique, and a split placement fails silently: the deployment reports Ready and chat completions return HTTP 200 with `content: null`. Measured on GB200: TCP across cliques 0.707 GB/s, NVLink inside one clique 1.7 to 2.2 GB/s. The documentation page records how to opt into the fabric and the clique requirement that comes with it.

The disaggregated target is authored as a Kustomize matrix. The base is portable. The `gke-rdma` variant claims the four RDMA networks that GKE GB200 node pools advertise.

Neither target is benchmarked, and the catalog records no performance claim. The runtime image gets its `artifacts` provenance block in a follow-up, once its source revision exists. This mirrors how #13798 and #14235 shipped the Inkling recipe.

- `scripts/kustomize-matrix.py check` — pass, with standalone Kustomize v5.8.1

The serving configuration in these manifests was qualified on a GB200 cluster. The aggregated shape passed 7 functional probes, including KV-aware routing across two workers. The disaggregated shape passed 8.

items.title: fix(discovery): report workers excluded from the routable set

labels.name: external-contribution
labels.description: Pull request is from an external contributor

items.body:
Source issue: [DYN-4236](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4236).

## Overview:

A vLLM worker started without `--kv_events_config` is registered by discovery, yet every request routed to its pool fails with `no endpoints available to route work`. The reported cause — that KV-event capability had become an admission requirement — does not hold for this worker shape: `KvSourceMembership` is handed only to the indexer's subscriber and never reaches the scheduler, and `kv_event_source_mode` is read after a worker is selected, to pick a transfer-hint source. Such a worker is admitted and simply scores zero KV overlap.

The real gap is that discovery says nothing when it drops a worker. **This does not restore routing for the reported deployment.** It makes the exclusion visible, so one re-run of that scenario names the branch to investigate.

## Details:

`lib/llm/src/discovery/runtime_configs.rs` holds the discovery-time admission predicate: a worker reaches the router's candidate set only if it appears in both the endpoint availability watch and the base model-card watch. The old `filter_map` kept the survivors and discarded any record of the rest.

This extracts that join into `join_available_instances_with_configs`, which also returns the instance ids that were available but carried no base runtime config, and logs one `WARN` naming the endpoint and those ids. The warning fires only when the excluded set changes, because `lib/kv-router/src/scheduling/queue.rs` borrows this watch on every selection. The previously silent `model_suffix` / `lora` guard now emits a `debug!` naming the instance and which reason applied.

Which workers are admitted does not change.

Reading the new warning: its presence means the instance was available and its base card was missing or dropped. Its absence rules out that branch only — hard availability, taints, and a mismatched router `--endpoint` all produce this failure with no warning — so please report the warning's presence or absence together with the router's resolved `--endpoint`.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`join_available_instances_with_configs` and its call site in `runtime_config_watch`, then the four new tests in the same file.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo check --manifest-path lib/bindings/python/Cargo.toml --all-targets`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings` — all exit `0`.
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib discovery::runtime_configs` — `8 passed; 0 failed`. Against the pre-change join semantics the new exclusion test fails on its assertion (`left: {}`, `right: {8}`).
- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router --lib scheduling` — `189 passed; 0 failed`, so the scheduler's candidate-set and eligibility tests are unaffected.
- `pytest -m "gpu_0 and integration and router" tests/router/test_router_e2e_with_mockers.py::test_mocker_kv_event_publisher_disabled_diagnostic` — the `[aggregated]` case passes: a real router and mocker workers with KV event publishing disabled return HTTP 200. The `[disaggregated]` case times out after 120 s, and fails identically at the branch point `ea39f8063` without this change.

items.title: fix(ext-proc): select standalone cache-salt forwarding by tokenizer backend

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Problem

Standalone EPP resolves an effective `cache_namespace` from the request body and headers, then uses it for KV-aware selection.

Today, its `PickResult` unconditionally uses the native-vLLM forwarding policy. That causes ext-proc to inject vLLM's top-level `cache_salt` extension (`dynamo-cache-salt:<namespace>`) even when standalone EPP uses the SGLang tokenizer/renderer.

SGLang does not currently have a compatible cache-salt request and KV-event contract. Forwarding the vLLM extension to it is therefore incorrect.

## Desired behavior

Derive cache-salt forwarding from the standalone tokenizer/renderer protocol:

- `VllmRender` -> `CacheSaltForwarding::NativeVllm`
  - Inject the resolved, Dynamo-prefixed top-level `cache_salt` for raw vLLM.
- `SglangRenderer` -> `CacheSaltForwarding::NativeSglang`
  - Keep the resolved namespace for Dynamo selection only.
  - Do not inject or overwrite `cache_salt` in the forwarded request body.
- Dynamo runtime continues using `CacheSaltForwarding::Preserve`; downstream workers resolve and tag the original cache-salt inputs.

This relies on the standalone configuration invariant that the tokenizer/renderer protocol matches the registered worker backend.

## Scope

This does not add end-to-end cache-salt isolation for raw SGLang. It prevents EPP from sending vLLM's extension to SGLang while preserving correct namespace-aware selection. SGLang cache-salt forwarding and matching KV-event representation should be investigated separately.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add `CacheSaltForwarding::NativeSglang`.
- Select the forwarding policy from `RendererProtocol` when constructing standalone `EppRouter`.
- `inject_body_extensions` receives a cache salt only for `NativeVllm`.
- Add focused coverage for the renderer-protocol-to-forwarding-policy mapping.

items.title: feat(gms/vllm): attach KV cache to persistent GMS pools
items.body:
## Overview:

This PR places vLLM's KV tensors in a GMS-owned persistent pool. A stable identity check ensures a shadow attaches only when the model and cache layout match exactly.

## Details:

- Derive a stable identity from model, KV layout, tensor geometry, and device mapping.
- Install vLLM KV tensors into daemon-owned persistent VMM allocations.
- Reject incompatible pools rather than interpreting old bytes under a new layout.
- Refuse shared-KV installation unless lease-aware vLLM block allocation is present.

### Why it is needed

Identity and attachment form one correctness boundary: a shadow may reuse physical KV only when its native representation matches.

### Stack boundary

This checkpoint introduces the attachment mechanism but deliberately does not activate it from normal `GMSWorker` startup. PR #13398 adds lease-aware block allocation, and PR #14583 then wires both mechanisms into production startup. Direct shared-mode installation at this checkpoint fails closed because two engines must never attach to writable KV without lease coordination.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`install_vmm_ipc_kv.py` for pool attachment and `kv_identity.py` for compatibility gating.

## Validation

- Identity and fail-closed installer suite: 23 passed.
- PR #13398 checkpoint, where the lease implementation becomes available: 32 focused tests passed.
- VMM-IPC byte-preservation suite: 2 passed locally on CUDA and is selected by the `pre_merge and none and gpu_1` CI lane.
- Cumulative daemon and vLLM suites pass.

items.title: feat(router): unify frontend and standalone selection core

labels.name: external-contribution
labels.description: Pull request is from an external contributor

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Summary

Unifies frontend, standalone SelectionService and EPP routing around one `SelectionCore` with shared scheduling, worker membership, KV indexing and session affinity. This removes the parallel runtime scheduler and makes reservation, catalog-update and affinity lifecycle behavior consistent across selection hosts.

This draft brings the complete aggregate-serving stack from [fork PRs #45](https://github.com/ishandhanani/dynamo/pull/45)–[#53](https://github.com/ishandhanani/dynamo/pull/53) to `ai-dynamo/dynamo:main`, implementing [DEP #14310](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/14310). It uses the exact head of [combined fork PR #55](https://github.com/ishandhanani/dynamo/pull/55), retains the existing stack for review history, and excludes the separate [DisaggCoordinator PR #40](https://github.com/ishandhanani/dynamo/pull/40).

### Implementation

- Embeds the shared selection partition in the frontend and routes every frontend selection through `SelectionCore::run_selection`; the frontend's own copy of the pipeline (index and shared-cache lookup, LoRA narrowing, transfer hints, booking) and the old `KvScheduler` are deleted, and selector generics and temporary adapters are replaced with `SelectionPolicySource` and `SelectionHost`.
- Shares worker registration through `WorkerCatalogSource` / `CatalogReconciler`, including EPP data-parallel ranks; metadata updates preserve surviving bookings and unchanged listeners.
- Uses one `Indexer` and `KvIndexSource` contract for event-driven, approximate and remote indexing, with `RuntimeIngress` and `ZmqDirectIngress` providing host-specific event transport.
- Moves enabled session-affinity tables into core partitions, scopes replica events by partition, and owns affinity leases in reservation records; the table owns the Hard/Soft commit that every host (frontend, standalone service, EPP) binds through; exposes affinity through the standalone service, Python API and EPP.
- Fixes reservation expiry, cancellation, worker scale-to-zero/rejoin and invalid TTL handling; core bookings are guarded by the queue's lifecycle lease so a dropped selection frees its booking; the frontend keeps lease-expiry ownership and starts replica ingress only after its lease manager is installed, replacing the deferred replica observer; removes redundant wrappers, arguments and repeated filtering.

<details>
<summary>Walkthrough</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Frontend[Frontend KvRouter] --> Core[SelectionCore partition]
  Standalone[SelectionService and EPP] --> Core
  Discovery[Runtime discovery or pod reflector] --> Catalog[CatalogReconciler]
  Catalog --> Core
  Events[RuntimeIngress or ZmqDirectIngress] --> Index[Shared Indexer]
  Index --> Core
  Core --> Scheduler[Scheduler and policy]
  Core --> Affinity[Partition affinity table]
  Core --> Reservation[Reservation record]
  Reservation --> Lease[Owned affinity lease]
```

### Selection and state ownership

`SelectionPolicySource` resolves the configured registry policy or an explicit factory when the partition is built. `SelectionHost` supplies the runtime-specific load, eligibility, shared-cache, telemetry and replication inputs while the core owns scheduling and bookings. Indexed overlap and optional shared-cache hits feed selection alongside caller constraints. LoRA narrowing preserves the caller's allow-set and allowed pin; structured session metadata takes precedence over the legacy flat session ID.

The same partition index serves initial selection, dequeue-time overlap refresh and routing-decision recording. Event transport remains behind the ingress interface: runtime recovery stays in the frontend ingress, and standalone ingress owns direct ZMQ worker subscriptions. Remote indexing reads the primary without opening local worker subscriptions.

### Membership and request lifecycle

`CatalogReconciler` applies desired worker snapshots, retries incomplete registration and removes withdrawn workers. Upserts prepare records before taking the mutation lock, so independent policy construction can proceed concurrently; committed updates reconcile only removed or changed ranks and endpoints. An empty partition keeps its index so a rejoined worker feeds the index the scheduler still holds.

A booked request with a session ID and no explicit pin or affinity target acquires the partition's binding before selection. The selected worker commits a new binding; a stale binding can be invalidated and rebound after worker withdrawal. Waiting for another initializer honors cancellation. Advisory selection reads existing bindings and projected load without queue admission, booking or affinity initialization.

The selection id is claimed in the reservation index before booking and the reservation is installed after the affinity commit, so a rejected commit leaves no booking behind. Explicit free and stale-record cleanup drop the reservation's affinity lease through the same ownership path. Standalone bookings retain periodic expiry; frontend bookings retain `RequestLeaseManager` expiry ownership, and inbound replica events start only once that manager exists. Enabled affinity is partition-scoped, preventing equal session IDs in different models or routing groups from colliding; frontend wrappers borrow that table and share replica initialization and coordinator lifetime.

### DEP feedback and remaining design differences

Tom's affinity ownership proposal is implemented at the partition boundary, but tables still initialize lazily when enabled rather than existing unconditionally. Builtin routing modes without a selection partition retain their host-owned table. EPP uses hard affinity because it cannot observe the actual dispatch outcome.

The other proposed host-boundary removals are not implemented in this draft. Availability and overload callbacks retain transport inhibition, immediate overload feedback, backend KV occupancy and the two-signal latch, which catalog and slot state alone do not contain. The prefill estimator still resides in `HostLoad`; moving it to partition construction remains outstanding.

Controller-aware LoRA filtering still carries `replica_set` and `is_active` semantics beyond loaded-adapter metadata. ModelManager still owns shared-cache subscriptions to preserve configuration gates, overrides and reconnect behavior; the proposed config-source/core-owned-client split remains outstanding. The LoRA scorer/plugin redesign was explicitly a follow-up. These are reviewed design differences, not resolved DEP comment threads.

The reservation lease leak, cross-partition affinity collision, sole-worker rejoin failure, metadata-update state loss and Python TTL panic were reproduced before their fixes.

</details>

## Validation

Validated source head: `b91015f183bc159e1fbf6968f2cc967cbbc0b23f`. The benchmark baseline and stack merge base are `ab58558c2dff28f4ff1ea4e219030eac5da3f48f`. Opening this upstream PR changes neither source nor tested tree.

At opening, upstream `main` was `7650b765fda7e411650393d3265d0a6ce0fb0b33`, 12 commits beyond the tested baseline, with one import conflict in `lib/llm/src/entrypoint/input/http.rs`. The branch has since merged `origin/main` at `464ea4f82a0c` (commit `8071b3e1c6`), resolving that conflict, and the validation below applies to the reviewed head `b91015f183` plus the review follow-up commits listed next.

### Review follow-up (after `b91015f183`)

Fixes for findings from the inline review, each as its own commit:

- Lock-order inversion between the reservation index and partition map that could wedge the standalone core (`efb4c7e7bd`).
- Worker completion marks are consumed without `router_replica_sync`, and the direct-ZMQ active-sequence ingress (`DYN_ROUTER_ACTIVE_SEQUENCE_DIRECT_ZMQ`, `DYN_ROUTER_ACTIVE_SEQUENCE_ZMQ_RCVHWM`, its metrics) is restored rather than removed (`533ff450aa`).
- The `standalone-slot-tracker` feature builds in isolation, with a pre-merge CI step for the isolated feature builds (`ab4c959628`).
- Discovered frontend workers without `max_num_batched_tokens` default to the scheduler's fallback capacity instead of becoming unschedulable (`0c0096d780`).
- Per-worker load gauges, router queue metric families and the prefill non-max-overlap observer are produced again (`76c4374177`, `e5fe3f00a1`).
- Core bookings are released when the caller drops the selection, when the selected worker drained while the request was queued, and a concurrent affinity failover keeps the rebound session lease (`960500e469`, `3003cb8ae0`); KV listeners lost to a cancelled worker update are re-registered and their stale index blocks purged (`92ea625801`, `b4a81a5d40`).
- Test hooks moved behind a `testing` feature; dead re-exports and `LoadEstimatorConfig::poll_interval` removed (`20c307dd86`).

Behavior changes relative to the reviewed head, all in the standalone service and EPP unless noted:

- A full session-affinity table routes the request without pinning instead of failing it (`ca0a0c6a1d`).
- Over-long `x-dynamo-session-id` values return 400 from the EPP instead of 503 (`17c73cc2b3`).
- An unreachable remote indexer maps to 503 `not_ready` instead of 500, with a 2 s connect timeout (`9493e06e2b`).

Docs corrected for the `kv_hint` envelope, builder method names, lru fallback, `advisory` being ignored by `select_and_reserve`, replication requiring a replica mesh, TTL bounds and `host_pinned` casing.

### Gate at head `b4a81a5d40` (merged with `origin/main` `464ea4f82a0c`)

- Offline replay parity (`.agents/skills/dynamo-kv-replay-parity`) was not rerun: `lib/kv-router/src/scheduling`, `sequences`, `lib/mocker` and `lib/bench` are byte-identical to the reviewed head `b91015f183`, and offline replay does not pass through `SelectionCore`, so the campaign would compare identical code.

- Rust suites: 1,115 KV-router tests, 2,420 LLM tests with no default features, and 154 EPP tests passed (3,689 total; three ignored). Strict core Clippy passed.

### Frontend cutover to the shared core (after `b4a81a5d40`)

Production-only line delta for these commits (non-test `.rs`, `#[cfg(test)]` modules stripped): +2,843 / −2,653, net +190; the frontend `kv_router.rs` alone lost 1,196 lines and `route_lookup.rs` is deleted, while the core gained the lease guard, claims, affinity commit and operation types.

Gate at head `25aea16655` (the stack fix `25aea16655` included):

- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router --features standalone-selection` (1,127 tests), `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib --tests` (2,672 lib tests plus integration binaries), `cargo test -p dynamo-ext-proc` (156 tests): all pass; isolated `cargo check --no-default-features --features standalone-slot-tracker` passes.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: pass. `cargo fmt --check`: pass.
- `lib/bindings/python` with `--features select-service`: select-service tests pass with explicit libpython linking.
- Dependent workspace crates (`dynamo-mocker`, `dynamo-bench`, `dynamo-backend-common`, `kvbm-consolidator`, the custom-policy examples and catalog): 468 tests across 34 binaries pass.
- `pytest tests/router/test_router_e2e_with_mockers.py` (bindings built with `kv-indexer,slot-tracker,select-service,aic-forward-pass`, etcd 3.5.21, nats-server 2.10.28): 50 passed, 6 skipped (the pre-existing TCP round-robin skip). The first run of this suite at `89785a3e7b` failed every disaggregated case: the frontend segfaulted with a stack overflow in `await_with_cleanup_policy`, whose state held the now-larger selection future three times under the prefill router's nesting. `25aea16655` pins the operation once in that wrapper and boxes the core selection future in the embedded host; a unit test bounds the selection future's size.

### Review round, structure cleanup and merge of main (after `25aea16655`)

- `e22fab5ee7`: the eleven review items on the previous head (DashMap guard before an await, direct `TieredQueryResponse` serialization, 8 MiB body limit on the hash routes, reservation drops outside the index lock, `Book`-only hash copy, LoRA filter intersected with its candidate set, replica writer id stored after the sink installs, pytest timeout marker, the no-op `register_workers` chain deleted, two-phase doc corrected).

- `bbd8412a91`: the frontend's request lease manager is built before the scheduler and passed directly as the partition observer; the late-bound observer shim is gone.
- `45383b4c9f`: merge of `main` at `0027a8ef0b` (75 commits). Every test added by the twelve main commits that touch the router, discovery, EPP and recovery paths is present and passes.

Gate at `45383b4c9f`: fmt, clippy `-D warnings` on kv-router (default and `standalone-selection` features), llm, ext-proc, bindings `cargo check --features select-service`; kv-router 1140, llm 2743, ext-proc 158, runtime routing policy 9; mocker e2e 50 passed / 6 skipped. GPU functional probes at this head (sa-b200, SGLang 0.5.19, Qwen3-0.6B; aggregated job 14430, disaggregated job 14401): all pass. Aggregated: health, prefix reuse routes 4/4 to the cached worker, distinct prompts spread over both workers, hard session sticky across unary and stream requests, explicit pin to the other worker rejected, cancelled stream then same-session completion, migration after SIGKILL of one worker with 8/8 in-flight streams completed and the survivor taking the next requests; plus the 49-completion smoke and the 34-completion standalone selector probe (catalog failover, scale-to-zero and rejoin). Disaggregated (1P+1D over NIXL): 12/12 requests carry a prefill id from the prefill pool and a decode id from the decode pool; prefix reuse, stickiness and cancellation hold.

### Structural review items (after the cleanup rounds)

The six structural threads from the review are addressed in this PR rather than deferred:

- `9e1e92a87b`, `d4be24436d`: a session commit that finds another request initializing the session joins that initialization and holds a lease on the new binding, instead of proceeding unpinned; a joiner that finishes first is uncounted again. The commit still never waits.
- `29b2b9c632`, `2dfc529eb2`: the worker-selection policy is constructed once per partition (was three times on the model-manager path); the inspected instance is the one that serves.
- `7b2f6c3faf`, `3cecd2af8d`: bookings read hint capability from the published partition snapshot instead of scanning the catalog, and deleted workers leave the catalog (they no longer appear in `GET /workers` as unschedulable).
- `9a18ffb109`, `4cc6f49acf`: a catalog snapshot reconciles as one batch with one publish per partition (a completed partition move still publishes immediately), continues past a failed record, and a failed snapshot is retried after five seconds unless a newer one arrives.
- `02165d72b1`, `27c03ee2a4`: the active-sequence ingress funnel is instrumented (queue depth, events applied, drain batches, per partition and worker type). At C1024 on 8 workers it drains 4 events per batch with depth 0 on every sample and no drops, so the single apply task is kept; the thread carries the numbers and the decision rule.

Each change has a test that fails without it; each commit was reviewed before landing.

### Cleanup rounds (after `45383b4c9f`)

Three targeted rounds to shrink the diff without losing a check. Every deleted test names the surviving test in its commit message, and each round was reviewed for lost assertions before landing.

- `5c2eb04504`: test-only shims (`find_best_match`, `find_best_match_details`, `query_prefill_worker`), dead consts and re-exports, the `kv_router/scheduler.rs` shim; six duplicate tests; 28 repeated core-test constructor literals folded into helpers.

Against the merged `main` commit `0027a8ef0b`: before the rounds +14,965 / −8,755 (net +6,210); after +14,399 / −9,461 (net +4,938). Of what remains, about 5,800 added lines are tests, benches and test data; the production growth is the frontend host over the shared core, the catalog and event-ingress reconcile that lets the frontend drive it, the reservation claim transaction, and the session-affinity replication.

### GPU functional validation at `25aea16655` (sa-b200, two B200 GPUs, SGLang 0.5.19, Qwen3-0.6B)

Release bindings built with `select-service`; frontend `--router-mode kv --kv-cache-block-size 16 --router-session-affinity-ttl-secs 60 --router-session-affinity-mode hard --migration-limit 3`; worker KV events on. Every probe attributes responses by `nvext.worker_id`.

items.title: [FEATURE]: Add dynamic-load validation for subagent group affinity

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Feature request

Add a controlled real-GPU validation for the `subagent-group-affinity` policy in
draft PR [#14521](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14521), focusing on
the trade-off between retaining a sibling group on a worker with a reusable KV
prefix and rebinding it to a less-loaded worker that may need to recompute the
prefix.

This issue is intended to establish evidence and acceptance criteria before
proposing a more complex routing mechanism. It does not assume that the current
policy is incorrect, and it does not initially request multi-worker replication
or eager prefix warming.

## Describe the problem you're encountering

PR #14521 keeps a policy-local binding from `parent_session_id` to one
worker/DP rank. A bound group remains on that worker while its
`active_requests` value is at or below `max_active_requests`. Once the threshold
is exceeded, the policy selects a strictly less-loaded eligible worker and
updates the group binding. Requiring a strictly lower load prevents movement
between equally loaded workers.

The remaining question is how this behaves when worker load changes between
sibling arrivals. A possible sequence is:

```text
child 1: parent P binds to worker A
child 2: A is above the threshold, so P rebinds to B
child 3: B becomes busy and A becomes less loaded, so P rebinds to A
child 4: A becomes busy, so P rebinds to C
```

Because KV state is normally local to a worker/cache domain, each transition to
a cold worker may require another full shared-prefix prefill. The strict load
comparison prevents equal-load oscillation, but the current tests do not cover
repeated transitions caused by alternating, strictly lower loads.

`active_requests` is also only a coarse proxy for queueing delay under
continuous batching. Several nearly completed requests can be cheaper than one
long decode, while recomputing a 16K or 32K prefix may cost more than waiting a
short time for a worker that already has the prefix.

The routing trade-off can be expressed conceptually as:

```text
stay_cost = estimated queueing cost on the worker with reusable KV
move_cost = target queueing cost + cold-prefix recomputation cost
```

An exact online estimate may not be available. The immediate goal is therefore
to measure the end-to-end result of the current threshold policy rather than to
introduce an unvalidated cost model.

### Existing evidence

I built an agent-tree measurement harness and ran 350 trials / 1,700 requests
using Dynamo 1.4.1, vLLM 0.26.0, exact 16,384- and 32,768-token prefixes, and
one worker per physical GPU on dual-RTX-4090 and eight-RTX-4090D systems.

- 115/115 physical-GPU KV-aware trials placed cold sibling groups across
  workers and computed one full prefix per worker touched.
- 50/50 physical-GPU session-affinity controls co-located the siblings and
  computed one full prefix per group.
- 120/120 strict single-worker trials computed one shared prefix, with no
  observed same-worker duplicate full prefill.
- For fan-out 8 with a 32K prefix, the eight-worker rows computed 262,152
  prefill tokens per trial, compared with 32,776 for the one-worker affinity
  control.

This supports a first-hop placement diagnosis for the tested single-host, idle
configuration, but it does not validate #14521 under background load and does
not establish that hard one-worker affinity is the production solution.

Related artifacts:

- Evidence and discussion: [#11343](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11343#issuecomment-5478778548)
- Existing benchmark contribution request: [#14045](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/14045)
- Benchmark branch: [`JasperChan929/dynamo:bench/agent-tree-sibling-placement`](https://github.com/JasperChan929/dynamo/tree/bench/agent-tree-sibling-placement)

## Proposed validation

Run the same exact-prefix sibling workload with the parent-aware policy disabled
and enabled, using identical capacity and background-load schedules.

### Initial scope

- one frontend and eight physical-GPU workers;
- fan-out 2/4/8;
- exact 16K/32K shared prefixes and one-token child suffixes;
- burst plus deterministic small-jitter arrival;
- cold unique prefix per trial;
- no background load as a control;
- balanced steady background load;
- one deliberately hot worker;
- an alternating-hotspot schedule that crosses the configured threshold between
  sibling decisions;
- the #14521 example threshold, followed by a small threshold sensitivity sweep
  only if the first comparison shows rebinding.

### Comparisons

1. Existing KV-aware routing without the parent-aware policy.
2. PR #14521 `subagent-group-affinity` with soft session affinity.
3. Shared-session affinity as a co-location/lower-bound-compute control, not as
   a proposed production policy.

Every child must have its own session ID and the siblings must carry one common
parent session ID in the policy-enabled row.

### Required observations

- ordered first-hop worker/DP-rank sequence for each parent;
- distinct physical-GPU workers touched per parent;
- full-prefix computations and duplicate-prefix copies per parent;
- prompt tokens, cached tokens, and computed prefill tokens;
- TTFT distribution, including tail latency;
- request completion and send skew;
- background-load schedule and worker/GPU topology;
- group transitions inferred from ordered worker selections;
- load observed at the routing decision, if exposed; otherwise mark it `TBD`.

### Questions the experiment should answer

1. Does #14521 continue to reduce physical cache domains and full-prefix copies
   under changing load?
2. How often does one parent group rebind, and can it return to a previously used
   worker?
3. Does a load-triggered move improve TTFT enough to offset cold-prefix
   recomputation?
4. How sensitive are the result and hotspot risk to `max_active_requests`?
5. Does the policy preserve completion and fallback behavior when its bound
   worker becomes ineligible?

## How the result would guide follow-up work

- If groups normally remain on one worker and prefix copies stay near one,
  retain the simple policy and avoid adding more routing state.
- If groups move occasionally and those moves improve latency, document the
  operating range and threshold sensitivity.
- If alternating load causes repeated rebinding and prefix recomputation,
  evaluate the smallest stabilizer first: a cooldown, hysteresis, or a bounded
  number of rebinds.
- Consider a small stable affinity set (for example, one primary and one
  standby) only if measurements show that a parent otherwise touches many cache
  domains. Preselecting a standby does not reserve its capacity or give it the
  prefix, so it should not be treated as zero-cost failover.
- Do not eagerly prefill every standby unless a separate experiment shows that
  the resilience benefit justifies deliberate duplicate computation and KV
  occupancy.
- After the single-frontend behavior is understood, test multiple frontends and
  multiple hosts separately because #14521's group map is policy-local.

## Alternatives considered

### Hard affinity

It minimizes duplicate prefix computation but can concentrate a wide fan-out on
one worker. The existing idle measurements do not show a TTFT improvement and
should not be interpreted as a production policy comparison.

### Immediate cost-aware routing

Comparing predicted queueing time with prefix recomputation cost is a promising
direction, but exact queue position and drain rate are not directly available
under continuous batching. Adding such a model before measuring the current
policy would introduce prediction error and additional scope without first
showing that threshold-triggered rebinding is a material problem.

### Multiple preselected workers

A bounded affinity set could cap the number of cache domains touched, but a
preselected worker may be busy by the time it is needed. Without reservation or
prefix warming it does not guarantee fast failover; with reservation or eager
warming it consumes capacity and intentionally creates extra prefix copies.
This should remain a measurement-driven follow-up rather than part of the
initial validation.

items.title: feat(router): ship a two-tier cost function as a worker-selection policy
items.body:
## Summary

Inspired by other routing policies in the wild, this PR adds `two_tier_cost_fn` to `lib/router-plugins/builtin`, a worker-selection policy that ranks workers on **two tiers** — active-request load first, then device-KV prefix overlap — instead of folding both into one additive cost the way Dynamo's built-in selector does.

The thresholds and selection order are the exact implementation ported from the experimental SGLang router's `cache_aware_zmq` policy, using Dynamo's authoritative device-KV overlap rather than that router's approximate cache history. Its thresholds are exposed as instance parameters defaulting to that router's values, so an instance with no `parameters` mapping reproduces it exactly. Unknown or out-of-range keys fail startup naming the key.

`custom-policy` is now enabled by default, so a stock build ships the policy and a deployment selects it from YAML with no rebuild and no custom image.

```yaml
worker_selection:
  aggregated: dynamo-two-tier-cost-fn
  instances:
    - name: dynamo-two-tier-cost-fn
      type: dynamo-two-tier-cost-fn
```

```bash
python3 -m dynamo.frontend --router-mode kv --router-policy-config worker-selection.yaml
```

For each eligible worker the policy reads device-KV overlap and active-request count, then takes the first tier that applies:

1. **Load tier** — if the active-request spread is greater than 32 **and** the largest count is more than 1.1 times the smallest, select the least-loaded worker. Both gates must hold, so load displaces cache affinity only when the imbalance is both large in absolute terms and disproportionate.
2. **Cache tier** — otherwise, if the largest device-KV overlap is strictly more than 50% of the request's block count, select the least-loaded worker among those holding that exact maximum overlap.
3. Otherwise, select the least-loaded worker.

## What changes

1. **The policy** — a module in `lib/router-plugins/builtin`, the crate holding the policies Dynamo ships. One module per policy.
2. **`custom-policy` becomes a default feature** of the Python bindings. It keeps its name and meaning; it is simply no longer opt-in.
3. **Shipped policies are separated from the replaceable catalog.** `dynamo-custom-policy-builtin` is a direct dependency of the bindings, not routed through the alias. A custom image still replaces only `dynamo-worker-selection-policy-catalog`, so its policies are registered *alongside* the shipped ones rather than displacing them, and a deployment can select either.

Shipped policies register first, so a catalog that reuses one of their type names fails startup on a duplicate registration instead of silently overriding it.

Because the shipped wheel already builds with `select-service` (`container/templates/wheel_builder.Dockerfile:596,612,625`), which enables `dynamo-kv-router/standalone-selection`, turning `custom-policy` on by default adds only this crate to the shipped dependency closure, and no new external dependencies.

Pre-merge clippy additionally lints `--no-default-features`, which the base job no longer covers now that `default` is non-empty.

## Validation

- `dynamo-custom-policy-builtin`: 7 tests — the cache tier outranking a less-loaded worker, the strict threshold comparison at exactly 50%, both load gates, duplicate rejection when a catalog reuses a shipped type name, and an end-to-end resolution of the documented YAML through the registry (the same path the bindings take at startup).
- **Coexistence check**: an external policy and catalog scaffolded by following the custom-policy guide verbatim, then linked through the `dynamo-worker-selection-policy-catalog` alias, builds with both the external crates and `dynamo-custom-policy-builtin` in the dependency closure. Replacing the alias does not drop the shipped policy.
- `dynamo-py3` clippy clean by default, with `custom-policy,select-service`, and with `--no-default-features`.
- Workspace clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, docs lint (0 errors), and pre-commit clean. CODEOWNERS coverage remains 100%.
- Confirmed against the shipped wheel's exact feature list (`kv-indexer,slot-tracker,select-service,mm-routing,aic-forward-pass,request-trace-s3`) that the crate is linked, since the container build does not pass `--no-default-features`.

Policy tests drive the real host selection path rather than the picker in isolation, because `WorkerCacheInput` and `WorkerLoadInput` have private fields and no public constructors.

## Documentation

- `configuration-and-tuning.md` gains the canonical **Worker-Selection Policies** section: available policy types, the `worker_selection` YAML, per-stage prefill/decode selection, and flag/environment precedence.
- The CLI KV-routing overview gains a runnable `--router-policy-config` walkthrough; the Kubernetes Frontend page gains a ConfigMap, volume mount, and Frontend args example.
- The custom worker-selection page points at that section instead of duplicating it, and states that a custom catalog registers alongside the shipped policies, so the write-your-own workflow carries no caveat about losing them.

## Known trade-off

Ties between equally ranked workers resolve on candidate row order, which the host leaves unspecified. This matches the ported implementation the benchmark below was produced with. Note that Dynamo's built-in selector instead samples uniformly among ties even at `router_temperature = 0`, so this policy can concentrate tied selections on one worker within a process. Tracked as a follow-up to change with its own before/after measurement rather than as an unmeasured edit to the benchmarked code.

## Not yet done

**No GPU A/B on this head.** Controlled validation of this policy measured -5.89% mean E2E, -11.27% TTFT, and prompt-cache hit 18.62% -> 24.09% against main-Dynamo. The policy logic here is unchanged from what produced that result, but it should be re-confirmed on this exact head before the PR leaves draft, along with a throughput check on the routing-host change: `custom-policy` being on by default moves the stock wheel from `RoutingHost` to `RoutingHost<WorkerSelectionPolicy>`.

items.title: feat(router): yield decode affinity under KV pressure

labels.name: external-contribution
labels.description: Pull request is from an external contributor

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Problem this solves

Hard session affinity preserves KV locality for multi-turn requests, but today an implicitly bound decode request remains pinned even when that data-parallel rank's projected active KV footprint is near capacity. The normal KV-aware selector cannot relieve the hot rank because the affinity binding is presented as a strict placement constraint. Long-lived sessions can therefore concentrate decode work on one rank while other eligible ranks retain headroom.

This change adds an opt-in pressure escape hatch for **implicit decode affinity only**. It keeps hard affinity as the default behavior and leaves explicit request pins strict.

## Summary

- Add the experimental `--router-decode-affinity-high-watermark` option and `DYN_ROUTER_DECODE_AFFINITY_HIGH_WATERMARK` environment variable.
- Before admitting a hard-affinity decode request, preview the bound rank's projected active blocks against its advertised KV capacity.
- When the projected fraction is strictly above the configured watermark, release only the current affinity lease and rerun normal unpinned KV selection.
- Preserve the stored session binding so later turns can reuse the original locality once pressure falls.
- Export `dynamo_component_router_decode_affinity_yields_total` to make the behavior observable.

The feature is disabled by default (`None`), and the accepted range is `0.0` through `1.0`.

## Workload evidence and motivation

The motivating case was GLM-5.2 NVFP4 serving a disaggregated, multi-turn coding workload across 32 backend GB200 GPUs. At concurrency 160, a matched end-to-end A/B changed only the pressure-aware affinity behavior and measured:

| Metric | Existing hard affinity | Watermark `0.70` | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Throughput per GPU | 19,748.50 tokens/s/GPU | 22,389.05 tokens/s/GPU | **+13.37%** |
| p90 per-user throughput | 90.933 tokens/s/user | 90.038 tokens/s/user | **-0.98%** |

The optimized configuration also retained a GSM8K score of 0.9682. This is evidence for the motivating topology, not a claim that `0.70` is a universal threshold: the appropriate watermark depends on model memory use, DP layout, request lengths, and the value of session locality.

## Behavior and safety

The pressure check runs only when all of the following are true:

- the request is in the decode phase;
- session affinity is in hard mode;
- the affinity target came from the stored session binding, not an explicit request pin;
- the request is not a query-only route preview; and
- a watermark was explicitly configured.

Explicit decode worker/rank pins, prefill routing, aggregated routing, soft affinity, and the default configuration are unchanged.

The check fails safe toward existing behavior:

- missing worker capacity or a below-threshold projection honors the pin;
- failure to inspect pressure logs a warning and honors the pin;
- cancellation remains cancellation rather than being swallowed;
- yielding drops the current lease without invalidating or rewriting the stored affinity binding; and
- reselection uses the existing KV scheduler, including its eligibility, allowlist, taint, and admission logic.

## Implementation notes

The pressure probe uses the scheduler's advisory no-admission path, so it does not reserve capacity or mutate active-request state. The compared load is the request-inclusive `potential_decode_blocks` projection already produced by the scheduler, divided by the selected worker rank's advertised `total_kv_blocks`. Selection is then performed exactly once through the normal admission path.

Configuration is wired consistently through the shared frontend/router CLI layer, Rust environment parsing and serialization, and the Python binding. The optional field is omitted from default serialization to preserve the existing default wire shape.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `(cd lib/bindings/python && cargo fmt -- --check)`
- `cargo check -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features decode_affinity -- --nocapture` (3 passed)
- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router dynamo_env_config_parses_canonical_settings -- --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router kv_router_config_preserves_v1_3_wire_compatibility -- --nocapture`
- `python3 -m compileall -q` for the touched Python configuration and test modules
- Added unit coverage for above-watermark reselection, below-watermark pin retention, explicit-pin preservation, CLI/environment propagation, binding validation, and default serialization compatibility.

## Limitations

- Enabling the feature adds one advisory selection pass for decode requests that already have an implicit hard-affinity target.
- It depends on active-block tracking and advertised KV capacity being representative of the decode rank. Missing capacity deliberately disables yielding for that request.
- It handles rank-local pressure; it cannot create capacity when every eligible rank is saturated.
- It does not permanently migrate the session binding. A later turn reevaluates the original binding and may yield again while pressure remains high.
- Threshold selection remains workload- and topology-specific; this PR intentionally provides no non-disabled default.

Adds Dynamo + vLLM serving recipes for SK Telecom's [`skt/A.X-K2`](https://huggingface.co/skt/A.X-K2) (688B MoE / 33B active, DeepSeek-V3-style MLA, block-scaled FP8 checkpoint, 256K context) on **32x H200**, plus the Fern recipe page and catalog entry.

Two targets, backed by a five-arm aggregated-vs-disaggregated and routing study at 16K ISL / 1K OSL with a 10K-token shared prefix:

| Target | GPUs | Parallelism | Routing | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `vllm/disagg-h200` | 32x H200 (2 prefill + 2 decode, 8 GPUs each) | prefill TP2×DP4 + EP / decode TP8 + EP, NIXL over UCX/RDMA | KV-aware (event-driven) | **Recommended** |
| `vllm/agg-h200` | 8x H200 per worker (4 workers measured) | TP8 + EP | Round-robin | Baseline |

> #13712 adds `recipes/a.x-k2/` for the **B200 NVFP4** checkpoint (`skt/A.X-K2-NVFP4`). This PR serves the FP8 checkpoint on Hopper. The two overlap on `recipes/a.x-k2/README.md` and `model-cache/`; happy to rebase onto whichever lands first.
>
> The vLLM 0.28-based worker image used for the study is under review for publication; a follow-up will add the public image and re-qualify the manifests.

## Details:

**Results (32x H200, `vllm bench serve` closed-loop, seed 42, single run per cell).** 
- W1 = 32 shared 10,240-token prefixes + 6,144 unique tokens per request
- W2 = 16,384 unique tokens (cold). Total tok/s counts input + output.

Prefill/decode disaggregation with KV-aware routing held constant (aggregated TP8 → 2P2D):

| Concurrency | W1 total tok/s | W2 total tok/s | W1 ITL p99 | W2 ITL p99 |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | 17,523 → 20,003 (+14 %) | 14,484 → 20,599 (+42 %) | 48 → 79 ms | 41 → 46 ms |
| 64 | 24,832 → 31,280 (+26 %) | 18,618 → 30,154 (+62 %) | 874 → 82 ms | 2,149 → 87 ms |
| 128 | 33,186 → 47,056 (+42 %) | 22,185 → 43,931 (+98 %) | 879 → 80 ms | 2,174 → 88 ms |
| 256 | 35,498 → 48,079 (+35 %) | 21,428 → stalled | 2,016 → 330 ms | 4,246 → stalled |

KV-aware routing with topology held constant (aggregated: round-robin → KV; 2P2D: random → KV), W1:

|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | +2 % | 0.95 → 2.01 s | +8 % | 2.74 → 1.38 s |
| 64 | +5 % | 0.96 → 2.22 s | +5 % | 2.70 → 1.56 s |
| 128 | +6 % | 1.14 → 4.25 s | +1 % | 3.51 → 1.82 s |

Takeaways, each reflected in the shipped manifests:

- Not deployed from this branch. Numbers come from the H200 study runs; the shipped AIPerf Job reproduces the same request shapes but was not the measurement tool.

## Related Issues

**This PR is NOT linked to an issue**:
- [x] Confirmed — no related issue

- **Worker image is a placeholder.** A.X-K2 needs the [SKT-AI vLLM fork](https://github.com/SKT-AI/vllm); the study ran a fork revision at vLLM 0.28.1rc1 on the Dynamo 1.4.2 runtime. Until then the public `axk2-v0.23.0` branch pairs with `vllm-runtime:1.3.0` and was not validated with these flags (`--kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune=False`, `--dyn-default-thinking-mode`). items.title: feat(router): order least-loaded routing by queued prompt tokens

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
> [!NOTE]
> **Stacked PR.** Targets `gluo/fixed-commit-prefill-card-router-mode`, not `main`, so the diff shows only this work. That base branch has no PR of its own yet; retarget this one to `main` once it lands.

## Summary

Least-loaded routing has only ever known *how many* requests a worker holds, never how large they are. A worker sitting on one 4k-token prompt therefore looks idler than one holding two 32-token prompts. Prefill cost tracks the prompt, not the request count, so that ordering inverts under a mixed-length workload.

This adds a second dimension to per-worker occupancy, gated behind `DYN_ROUTER_LEAST_LOADED_TOKEN_AWARE`:

```bash
DYN_ROUTER_LEAST_LOADED_TOKEN_AWARE=1 python -m dynamo.frontend --router-mode least-loaded
```

With it set, the router orders workers by the **total prompt tokens of their in-flight requests**, using the in-flight **request count only to break ties**. With it unset, behavior is unchanged.

### How it works

`RoutingOccupancyState` gains a `queued_tokens` map (one atomic per worker) parallel to the existing `counts`, and `increment` now returns an `OccupancyLease` carrying `Arc`s to *both* counter cells plus the weight it charged, so release is symmetric across all three paths — permit drop, response-stream completion, and `retarget` when transport fallback moves a request mid-flight.

Selection reads a `RouteLoad { queued_tokens, requests }` whose **field order is the comparison order**, so derived `Ord` gives tokens-then-count for free:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
pub(crate) struct RouteLoad {
    pub(crate) queued_tokens: u64,
    pub(crate) requests: u64,
}
```

`PushRouter::with_load_weight` injects the per-request weight (following the existing `MultimodalCacheKeyExtractor` pattern). The two hops that carry a tokenized request — the frontend's preprocessed-request router and the prefill hop — supply `PreprocessedRequest::prompt_token_count`.

### Behavior when the flag is off

`queued_tokens` stays 0 everywhere, so the `Ord` degenerates to exactly today's request-count ordering. The weight extractor is not even called. Power-of-two-choices and device-aware-weighted read only the request-count component, so **neither changes in either configuration**.

### Deliberate scope limits

- **Untokenized hops keep request-count ordering.** Embeddings, classify, pooling, and the chat/completions routers that tokenize in the backend have no prompt length available at routing time. They weigh 0 rather than being given an estimate. Documented in the router guide.
- **The weight is fixed at admission.** It is the prompt length; it does not grow with generated output and does not model KV footprint. This is prefill-shaped accounting, not a substitute for KV routing.
- **The flag is process-wide and cannot be overridden per hop.** See below.

## Validation

**Unit** — `cargo test -p dynamo-runtime --lib` 594 passed; `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib` 2086 passed. `cargo clippy --workspace --no-deps --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo fmt` and `pre-commit` clean over the commit range.

New unit coverage: token ordering with request-count tie-break, weights-off degeneration, lease release returning both counters to zero, `retain` pruning token entries for departed workers, stale-lease isolation after a worker is re-added, env-var boolean parsing, P2C staying token-blind, and the extractor not running when the state is not token-aware.

**End-to-end** — a real `dynamo.frontend --router-mode least-loaded` against two real `dynamo.mocker` workers (file discovery + TCP request plane, so no etcd or NATS). The scenario holds a 4000-token prompt open on one worker and a 4-token prompt on the other, leaving both tied at exactly one in-flight request, then sends 10 short probes one at a time:

| Configuration | probes to short-prompt worker | to long-prompt worker |
|---|---|---|
| `DYN_ROUTER_LEAST_LOADED_TOKEN_AWARE=1` | **10** | 0 |
| unset | 4 | 6 |

The two parameterizations assert **mutually exclusive** outcomes, so a pass on both is what shows the flag is doing the work rather than the scenario passing for an unrelated reason. Stable across 4 runs.

Per `tests/router/CLAUDE.md`, the scenario lives in `tests/router/common.py` as `_test_least_loaded_token_aware` with a thin parameterized wrapper in `test_router_e2e_with_mockers.py`, and asserts through `nvext.worker_id` rather than log parsing.

**Not covered:** real engines (mockers only), the prefill hop specifically (the e2e exercises the frontend hop; both take the same weight from the same call), and fleet scale. The scenario is backend-agnostic, so pointing it at vLLM/SGLang is a thin wrapper away.

## Reviewer notes

**Why the diff spans 16 files.** The load metric was a scalar `u64` produced in `client.rs`, passed as `impl Fn(u64) -> u64` through `picker.rs`, and consumed at four selection sites in `push_router.rs`. Widening it to a pair is one type change whose fan-out is every producer, consumer, and test assertion. Roughly 250 production lines vs 310 test lines across those three files; the rest is a new type, an env constant, two re-export lines, four ~8-line wiring edits, and docs.

The smaller alternative — packing both values into one `u64` (`tokens << 20 | count`) and leaving every signature alone — would touch ~3 files. It was rejected because it corrupts ordering silently on overflow: a 1M-token prompt or >1M in-flight requests wraps into the neighbouring field and inverts the comparison with no error, which is precisely the failure mode this feature exists to prevent.

**Known tension worth a decision.** This branch is stacked on work whose purpose is making the prefill hop's routing configurable *per hop* from the prefill card. The flag added here is deliberately **not** per-hop: it is read once per process via `LazyLock`, and the only non-test construction path reaches it through `RoutingOccupancyState::default()`. `PrefillAdvertisement` carries nothing that can override it, so a prefill card can advertise *that* it wants `least-loaded` but not *how* least-loaded orders workers. You cannot run prefill token-aware and decode request-count.

An env var was chosen because the request allowed it, but making it card-overridable fits the existing seam: add the flag to `RouterConfig` so it rides the advertisement, then pass it into `get_or_create_routing_occupancy_state` (currently `&Endpoint` only) so per-endpoint state is built with the resolved per-hop value. `RoutingOccupancyState::new(bool)` already exists. The wrinkle is that state is shared per endpoint across routers, so two routers disagreeing about the same endpoint needs a defined winner — first-construction-wins, or reject the mismatch. Happy to do this if reviewers prefer it.


---

## Supplement: prior art in TensorRT-LLM ADP routing

Read from [`adp_router.py`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/scheduler/adp_router.py) on `main`. Included as motivation: the ordering rule this PR adopts is already the production choice for attention-DP load balancing in TensorRT-LLM.

**The ordering key matches exactly.** `DefaultADPRouter` builds a min-heap of `HeapVal(num_tokens, num_requests, rank, ...)`. As a namedtuple that orders lexicographically — tokens primary, request count as tie-break — which is precisely this PR's `RouteLoad { queued_tokens, requests }` with derived `Ord`. Its own docstring:

> Balance remaining unscheduled requests across ranks using a min-heap keyed on `(num_active_tokens, num_active_requests)`, so ranks with fewer tokens get more requests.

Same metric, too: `sum(req.py_orig_prompt_len for req in active_requests)` is summed prompt length.

**What this PR deliberately does not reproduce:**

- **Longest-first batch packing.** TRT-LLM sorts a *batch* of pending requests by token count descending (`counted.sort(key=..., reverse=True)`) before heap-popping — LPT bin-packing, and the main source of its balance quality. A network router dispatching per request on arrival has no batch to sort. Greedy-on-arrival is strictly weaker on the same metric.
- **Per-rank capacity cap.** TRT-LLM drops a rank from the heap once `num_requests >= expected_num_active_requests` (fair-share soft cap, floored at the busiest rank, capped at `max_num_active_requests`). Least-loaded here keeps stacking onto the minimum. This is the cheapest gap to close — it is local to the picker and needs no batching.
- **Ground-truth state.** TRT-LLM recomputes rank state each iteration from live active requests and allgathers it. This PR maintains a router-side lease counter: a belief about the worker that can drift, and is blind to in-engine queueing, preemption, and chunked prefill.
- **DP-rank granularity.** ADP routing targets attention-DP ranks *inside* one engine. `RouteTarget` carries a `dp_rank`, but `CandidateView::Workers` constructs `RouteTarget::worker(id)` with `dp_rank: None`, so least-loaded addresses worker instances only.

**Two other things also called "ADP", and out of scope here:**

- `KVCacheAwareADPRouter` scores `(req_tokens - prefix_match) + weight * normalized_load` with a cache-discounted token count (`max(orig_prompt_len - cached_tokens, 0)`). This PR charges raw prompt length with no cache credit; cache-aware placement is the KV router's job.
- The [ADP Balance Strategy](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/docs/source/blogs/tech_blog/blog10_ADP_Balance_Strategy.md) (`timeout_iters` / `batching_wait_iters`) deliberately *delays* scheduling to phase-align ranks — reported 33% throughput and balance ratio 54% → 88%, at a TTFT cost. That is iteration-level in-engine scheduling and is not reachable from a network router.

**Summary for reviewers:** this PR adopts the ADP ordering rule at worker granularity, not the ADP algorithm. The fair-share cap is the natural follow-up.

# 1.5 - 1.7 roadmap (Sep - Nov '26)

Hi Dynamo developers!

We wanted to share the Dynamo roadmap for the next three releases (1.5 - 1.7). This roadmap picks up where the [1.2 - 1.4 roadmap](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/9178) left off.

This window is organized around five initiatives: **Reinforcement Learning**, **Agents**, **Multimodality**, **Performance Tuning**, and **Developer Experience**. We recommend reading the release plan summaries first to get an overview, then jumping to the initiative you care about :)

## Table of Contents

- [Timeline](#-timeline)
- [Release Plan Summaries](#-release-plan-summaries)
- [Detailed Roadmap categorized by key initiatives](#-detailed-roadmap-categorized-by-key-initiatives)
  - [1. Reinforcement Learning (and scaling)](#-1-reinforcement-learning-and-scaling)
    - [Reinforcement Learning: Turning Dynamo into the rollout engine for RL post-training](#reinforcement-learning-turning-dynamo-into-the-rollout-engine-for-rl-post-training)
    - [Planner: Intelligent autoscaler to adhere to SLAs](#planner-intelligent-autoscaler-to-adhere-to-slas)
    - [Grove: Kubernetes-native AI inference orchestration](#grove-kubernetes-native-ai-inference-orchestration)
    - [Fault Tolerance](#fault-tolerance-built-in-inference-recovery-and-resiliency-to-keep-dynamo-deployments-stable-and-recoverable-in-production)
    - [Snapshot](#snapshot-criu-based-gpu-process-checkpoint-and-restore)
    - [Model Express](#model-express-fast-gpu-to-gpu-weight-transfer-over-rdma-for-autoscaling-fault-tolerance-rl-weight-sync-and-model-lifecycle-management)
  - [2. Agents](#-2-agents)
    - [Agents](#agents)
    - [Routing](#routing)
    - [KV Caching](#kv-caching)
  - [3. Multimodality](#-3-multimodality)
    - [Image and video](#image-and-video)
    - [Speech](#speech)
    - [Offline / Batch Inference](#offline--batch-inference)
  - [4. Performance Tuning](#-4-performance-tuning)
    - [AISimulate](#aisimulate)
  - [5. Developer Experience](#-5-developer-experience)
    - [Router EPP](#router-epp)
    - [Sidecar](#sidecar)

## 🗓️ Timeline

| 📦 Release      | 1.5.0    | 1.6.0     | 1.7.0    |
|--------------|---------|---------|---------|
| 🗓️ Planned date | 9/16/26 | 10/21/26 | 11/18/26 |

Patch releases follow roughly two weeks after each minor release: 1.5.1 on 9/30/26, 1.6.1 on 11/4/26, and 1.7.1 on 12/2/26.

## 📦 Release Plan Summaries

**1.5.0 — 9/16/26**

* **Reinforcement Learning (and scaling)**
  * RL integrations land upstream across NeMo RL, Prime-RL, SLIME, Miles, and veRL, with some benchmarks. The veRL and NeMo RL integrations are already complete.
  * Elastic EP gets its Kubernetes lifecycle contract, and Planner gets a repeatable evaluation harness in Planner Gym.
  * Snapshot graduates out of the monorepo into a versioned release.
  * Model Express defines the weight lifecycle semantics that reliable rank replacement depends on.
* **Agents**
  * Out-of-the-box Router performance improves against Moonshot and AgentX traces.
  * DRAM-to-DRAM distributed KV cache ships for vLLM and SGLang.
* **Multimodality**
  * Encode/prefill/decode disaggregation gains frontend decoding support, and the frontend picks up optimized JPEG decoding, video decoding, and video KV routing for Qwen models.
  * A deployable cascaded speech pipeline (ASR → LLM → TTS) lands with OpenAI-compatible realtime transcription sessions and incremental audio streaming.
  * The initial llm-d Batch Gateway integration lands, benchmarked across direct, sync, and async paths.
  * Initial integration example with [M*](https://github.com/mstar-project/mstar), modular serving system for multimodal models, with the integration living out-of-tree in the M* repository.
* **Performance Tuning**
  * AIConfigurator and Dynamo's simulation stack unify as **AISimulate**, a standalone product with `predict` and `recommend` commands and a scheduler-aware replay engine that closes the TTFT gap.
* **Developer Experience**
  * The Router moves toward a runtime-free architecture, usable with existing vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM deployments behind a Kubernetes Gateway, with EPP and custom-deployment parity.
  * The Dynamo Sidecar lets stock engine images run unmodified, with image input support for vLLM.

**1.6.0 — 10/21/26**

* **Reinforcement Learning (and scaling)**
  * Fault tolerance and RL converge on ModelExpress-assisted recovery for rollouts and rank replacement.
  * Planner moves into a production loop with KEDA.
  * Grove adds job support and cross-workload bin-packing.
  * Elastic EP moves from lifecycle contract to production deployment, with traffic drain and GPU return to the scheduler.
* **Agents**
  * Routing gains two-stage global routing, SLA-aware heterogeneous pool selection, and session/KV-aware affinity.
  * A session-aware prefix indexer lands router-side for agentic workloads.
  * KV cache tiering extends to SSD and remote storage.
* **Multimodality**
  * Video EPD support arrives for the vLLM backend, 
  * Per-request frame sampling control.
  * Recipe for co-serving multiple small models on one GPU.
  * Speech streaming survives worker failure with minimal interruption, and the full Batch Gateway + Async Processor deployment lands with end-to-end coverage.
* **Performance Tuning**
  * AISimulate completes its cutover and starts publishing a per-release prediction-accuracy scorecard.
* **Developer Experience**
  * Both Router EPP and the Sidecar are hardened for LLM use cases across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.
  * The Router extends to discovering and routing across native-engine workers, keeping native-runtime performance.
  * Sidecar image input extends to SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.

**1.7.0 — 11/18/26**

* **Reinforcement Learning (and scaling)**
  * Global Planner takes on multi-deployment capacity balancing and EnginePool/ComputeDomain placement.
  * Elastic EP adds multi-node topology, gang sizing, and NVLink/NVL72 locality.
  * Fault tolerance covers lost-node and lost-rank recovery with no-stranded-capacity guarantees.
  * Snapshot expands to multi-node placement and rendezvous contracts.
  * Model Express handles resharding and multi-cluster weight distribution.
* **Agents**
  * Router extensibility opens up filter, scorer, and picker plugin APIs.
* **Multimodality**
  * The Rust frontend gains optimized media preprocessing, and Planner takes on peak and off-peak SLA management for speech.
  * The batch surface expands to multimodal requests and additional endpoints, and Planner and llm-d Async begin sharing interactive and batch capacity under a single SLA budget.
* **Developer Experience**
  * Sidecar video input lands for SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and audio input support arrives.

---

# 🗺️ Detailed Roadmap categorized by key initiatives

## 🎓 1. Reinforcement Learning (and scaling)

RL post-training efficiency can be improved with Dynamo. DynamoPlanner, Grove, Fault Tolerance, Snapshot, and Model Express components are the scaling substrate it depends on — each is independently useful on their own, but they're sequenced so that a production RL rollout can run elastically at fleet scale.

* **Reinforcement Learning: Turning Dynamo into the rollout engine for RL post-training**
  * **[1.5] Integration and benchmark baseline**
      * Upstream Dynamo + ThunderAgent integrations across NeMo RL, Prime-RL, SLIME, Miles, and veRL.
      * Standardize the streaming `/generate` path, validate P/D disagg at higher concurrency, and remove trace-dumping overhead before publishing performance claims.
  * **[1.5 - 1.7] RL platform dependencies**
      * **Model Express** for delta-weight sync and Experience Transfer between trainer and rollout workers.
      * **Fault Tolerance** for stalled-job recovery, incorrect-weight-update detection, checkpoint and model-version recovery, and safe retry/failover.
      * **Grove / Kubernetes** for dynamic worker discovery, gang-aware launch and termination, autoscaling, drain and replacement, trainer/rollout capacity transitions, and integration with Ray and RL frameworks.
      * **Planner / Router** for straggler-aware scheduling, engine-fullness curves, cache- and session-aware routing, and trace-driven simulation.
  * **[1.6] Production RL workflows**
      * Dynamic worker discovery, streaming partial rollouts, ModelExpress delta sync, Experience Transfer, and recovery from stalled jobs or incorrect weight updates.
  * **[1.6 - 1.7] Tail-aware and elastic RL**
      * Productize straggler-aware scheduling, richer trace metadata, reusable rollout simulation, and cache/session-aware routing.
      * Elastic disaggregated RL with KV cache managers

* **Planner: Intelligent autoscaler to adhere to SLAs**
  * **[1.5] Planner Gym and AISimulate foundation**
      * Establish repeatable Planner evaluation using real workload traces, ForwardPassMetrics, and scheduler-aware simulation.
  * **[1.6] Production Planner loop**
      * Use Router Gym / AISimulate and KEDA to validate scaling and policy changes against real deployments before they ship.
      * Support Elastic EP scale decisions, engine-pool membership, traffic drain, safe retirement, and GPU return-to-scheduler semantics.
      * Focus on Batch/offline inference support via throughput-based scaling
  * **[1.7] Global Planner and fleet-aware scaling**
      * Productionize Global Planner for multi-pool capacity balancing, EnginePool/ComputeDomain placement, Elastic EP gang and topology decisions, NVLink/NVL72 locality awareness, and fleet reshaping.
  * **[1.5 - 1.7] Planner platform stabilization**
      * Plugin APIs for custom scaling logic, bring-your-own traces, ForwardPassMetrics across all backends, heterogeneous placement, multi-pool RL rate matching, and self-tuning policies.

* **Grove: Kubernetes-native AI inference orchestration**
  * **[1.6] Coherent rolling updates end-to-end with Dynamo**
  * **[1.6] Job Support**
      * Support terminal states and gang termination.
      * Bin-pack GPUs with jobs and inference deployments to support cross-workload scheduling.
  * **[1.6] Elastic EP production deployment**
      * Support externally launched vLLM/SGLang paths, including traffic drain, pod deletion and replacement, and return of idle GPUs to the Kubernetes scheduler.
  * **[1.7] Elastic EP topology and fleet scale-out**
      * Multi-node placement, EnginePool/ComputeDomain semantics, gang sizing, NVLink/NVL72 locality, and cross-pod MNNVL.
      * Fleet reshaping, plus a TensorRT-LLM extension point once the backend lifecycle is ready.

* **Fault Tolerance: Built in inference recovery and resiliency to keep Dynamo deployments stable and recoverable in production**
  * **[1.5 - 1.6] Recovery contract**
      * Define failure modes and SLOs for stalled jobs, incorrect weight updates, checkpoint and model-version recovery, Elastic EP node/rank replacement, and traffic correctness during recovery.
  * **[1.6] ModelExpress-assisted recovery**
      * Validate recovery for RL rollouts and Elastic EP replacement using ModelExpress weight transfer, with measured detection, rebuild, downtime, and GPU-reclamation behavior.
  * **[1.7] Fleet-scale resilience**
      * Extend to lost-node and lost-rank recovery, interrupted rollouts, GPU Memory Service / Snapshot / WideEP acceptance tests, and no-stranded-capacity guarantees.

* **Snapshot: CRIU-based GPU process checkpoint and restore**
  * **[1.5] Standalone release and baseline**
      * Graduate Snapshot out of the Dynamo monorepo into a versioned alpha/beta release.
      * Validate single-node checkpoint/restore, readiness gating, identity rebinding, structured failure reporting, and cold-start / warm-restore / failover measurements. Multi-GPU remains experimental until the Snapshot lifecycle and required CUDA integration dependencies close.
  * **[1.5] Kubernetes and operator hardening**
      * Close snapshot-agent and operator reconciliation issues seen in deploy tests, including stale observed generation, volume detach, ConfigMap and image-pull-secret propagation, and TensorRT-LLM checkpoint timeouts.
      * Complete containerd / CRI-O / OpenShift, seccomp and io_uring, PVC and namespace, and privileged-agent vs. restricted-workload guidance.
  * **[1.6] Storage-neutral transfer boundary**
      * Upstream the CRIU APIs needed by the page-broker path and replace Snapshot-local NIXL/POSIX transfer plumbing with a transfer-neutral custom-storage boundary.
      * Validate CUDA virtual-address and graph restoration, timeout/cancellation/failure semantics, and GPU Memory Service / Model Express memory ownership without duplication.
  * **[1.6 - 1.7] Multi-GPU and multi-node expansion**
      * Productize POSIX-FD and multicast topology replay, then define multi-node Kubernetes placement, identity, and rendezvous contracts.
      * FABRIC/MNNVL is evaluated only behind explicit topology and authorization gates.

* **Model Express: Fast GPU-to-GPU weight transfer over RDMA for autoscaling, fault tolerance, RL weight sync, and model lifecycle management**
  * **[1.5] Weight lifecycle foundation**
      * Define registry, loader, broadcast, and weight-version semantics for reliable engine and Elastic EP rank replacement.
      * Benchmark delta transfer.
  * **[1.6] Production transfer workflows**
      * Move delta-weight transfer and Experience Transfer from API capability to a production RL run.
      * Define add-rank / remove-rank weight-sync and replacement semantics for Elastic EP.
  * **[1.6] Speculative decoding draft model support**
      * Transfer target and draft models together in a single P2P operation.
  * **[1.7] Fleet-scale weight distribution**
      * Expand to resharding, multi-cluster updates, and reliable weight synchronization across Elastic EP fleet changes and interrupted or restarted rollouts.

---

## 🕵️ 2. Agents

Agentic workloads stress different parts of the stack than single-turn serving: long-lived sessions, bursty tool-call gaps, and prefix reuse across turns. This initiative covers the agent runtime itself plus the routing and KV caching work that makes agent traffic efficient.

* **Agents**
  * **[1.5] CPU orchestration for agents**
      * Testing against agent sandbox and environment substrates.
  * **[1.6] Session-aware prefix indexer**
      * Per [DEP #13279](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13279), an opt-in router-adjacent index that maps KV blocks to session identities and their in-session lineage, so the router can make session-aware policy decisions for agentic workloads. Working end-to-end with vLLM and SGLang, with a portable contract that only requires an engine to emit session-aware KV events.
  * **[1.7] Third-party KV store integration**
      * A worked example wiring agentic workloads to an external KV store with cache hints.

* **Routing**
  * *Router API work, and EPP and custom-deployment parity, are tracked under [Developer Experience](#-5-developer-experience).*
  * **[1.5] Out-of-the-box Router performance improvements**
      * Improve default Router performance without hand-tuning, measured against Moonshot and AgentX traces.
  * **[1.6] Global Router two-stage routing**
      * Standardize pool selection followed by worker selection across both single-cluster and multi-cluster deployments, without introducing an unnecessary third cluster-routing hop.
  * **[1.6] SLA-aware heterogeneous routing**
      * Account for request-level SLA requirements, live TTFT/ITL feedback, pool saturation, topology, parallelism, and performance predictions when selecting between heterogeneous pools.
  * **[1.6] Session- and KV-aware routing**
      * Soft-sticky session affinity and a portable session-aware KV contract across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, benchmarked against round-robin and existing sticky-session baselines.
  * **[1.7] Router extensibility**
      * Filter, scorer, and picker plugin APIs so deployments can add cost-, topology-, cache-, or policy-aware routing.

* **KV Caching**
  * **[1.5] DRAM-to-DRAM distributed KV cache**
      * Distributed KV cache with support for vLLM and SGLang.
  * **[1.6] SSD and remote storage support**
      * Extend the distributed KV cache tiering to SSD and remote object storage backends.

---

## 🎬 3. Multimodality

Beyond text: image, video, speech, ensembles, and batch. This initiative covers everything that isn't a single-modality LLM request, from disaggregated encode/prefill/decode through offline batch processing.

  * **MStar Integration** - initial integration ([#13817](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13817)) followed by deeper integration through routing, observability signals, and disaggregation
  * **Encode / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation**
      * [1.5] EPD deep-dive blog post.
      * [1.5] EPD with frontend decoding support.
      * [1.6] Video EPD support for the vLLM backend (the SGLang backend is already supported).
  * **Image and video inference**
      * [1.5] Optimized frontend JPEG decoding via libjpeg-turbo ([#11157](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/11157)).
      * [1.5] Frontend video decoding.
      * [1.5] Video KV routing for vLLM backend.
      * [1.5] Video KV routing for Qwen models.
      * [1.6] Video KV routing for SGLang backend.
      * [1.6] Per-request frame sampling control.

* **Speech**

      * Client-managed turn detection support.
      * OpenAI-compatible transcription sessions on `/v1/realtime`, including streaming audio, transcript events, and session affinity.

  * **[1.6] Resilient speech streaming**

  * **[1.7] Planner support for speech**
