      * Land the initial llm-d Batch Gateway integration and benchmark direct Dynamo, Batch sync, and Batch + Async paths.
      * Validate endpoint parity, identify missing links, and land isolated upstream durability fixes.
  * **[1.6] Full Batch Gateway + Async Processor deployment**
      * Repeatable deployment and end-to-end coverage, the production-critical durability work, and any endpoint support the 1.5 validation shows is missing.
  * **[1.7] Expanded batch surface**
      * Multimodal request support, additional endpoints as the community asks for them, and potentially Parquet input. Scoped based on community demand.
  * **[1.7] SLA-driven shared capacity**
      * Orchestrate shared interactive and batch capacity through Planner and llm-d Async.

---

## ⚡ 4. Performance Tuning

Getting a Dynamo deployment to the right configuration — and knowing what performance to expect before provisioning hardware. This initiative covers the simulation stack that replaces guess-and-check tuning.

* **AISimulate**
  * **[1.5] AIConfigurator and Dynamo's simulation stack unify as AISimulate**
      * AIConfigurator's engine performance modeling and Dynamo's scheduler-aware simulation (Mocker/replay) become one product. `aisimulate predict` evaluates a configuration and `aisimulate recommend` searches for a better one, with `--stack engine|dynamo` across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.
      * Ships as a standalone repository with an independently installable core: engine-only users run with no Dynamo dependency, and Dynamo integrates through adapters. Existing AIConfigurator packages, imports, and CLI keep working with deprecation warnings and a migration guide.
  * **[1.5] Scheduler-aware simulation closes the TTFT gap**
      * Replay simulation of scheduling, batching, and queueing replaces correction-factor-based TTFT estimation, tracking measured hardware closely at the high concurrencies where op-composition diverges most.
  * **[1.5] Forward-pass-metrics prediction debuts on vLLM**
      * A new prediction backend learns from forward-pass metrics measured on live engines, selectable alongside the existing op-based predictor. It launches with priority models and ships its measurement data as versioned assets.
  * **[1.5 - 1.6] Coverage expansion**
      * New frontier-model support and accuracy gap mitigation.
      * Model-agnostic large-scale expert parallelism, WideEP for vLLM, pipeline parallelism, elastic EP, and SGLang chunked pipeline parallel.
  * **[1.6] Cutover complete, accuracy published**
      * AISimulate becomes the single product surface; the AIConfigurator repository archives with compatibility shims so nothing breaks. Forward-pass-metrics prediction extends to SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.
      * A per-release prediction-accuracy scorecard by model, hardware, and backend, validated outside-in against published Dynamo recipe results.
  * **[1.6 - 1.7] Community-fed accuracy and self-service calibration**
      * A contribution path for community-measured forward-pass metrics with provenance and quality gates, expanding model and hardware coverage beyond what any one lab can measure.
      * A supported bootstrap workflow (collect, validate, register, predict) for hardware and models not yet covered, plus local calibration that learns per-environment correction factors as a versioned artifact. Calibrated and uncalibrated results are reported distinctly.

## 🛠️ 5. Developer Experience

Making Dynamo easier to adopt. Both workstreams below share a goal: let teams get Dynamo's routing and performance benefits **without adopting the full Dynamo runtime or rebuilding their engine images**. This section covers the roadmap through 1.7; the broader developer-experience plan — tool-call parsing, nightly artifacts, documentation restructuring, and community governance — is tracked in [#11821](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11821).

* **Router EPP**
  * **[1.5] Runtime-free routing architecture**
      * Separate routing decisions from any specific request plane or worker runtime, so that KV indexing, scheduling, and load/overlap scoring are owned independently of protocol handling and worker discovery.
      * Discover raw engine workers through Kubernetes reconciliation — watching `InferencePool` and matching pods — rather than self-registration, with worker metadata supplied via environment variables. This lets the Router deploy behind a Kubernetes Gateway through the Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE / Envoy `ext_proc`).
      * Factor the routing stack into modular, runtime-free components (KV indexing, load/overlap scoring, scheduler queue, peer sync) and improve the experience of deploying the Router via GAIE and Dynamo's EPP.
      * [DEP #11661](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11661) proposes embedding Dynamo's `SelectionService` directly in the Endpoint Picker Plugin, so teams get KV-aware and load-aware routing for raw OpenAI-compatible backends behind a Kubernetes Gateway without adopting the Dynamo runtime.
  * **[1.5] EPP and custom-deployment parity**
      * Make Router adoption consistent across EPP, Kubernetes-native discovery, and custom deployment paths.
      * Complete class-aware request shedding, load-based admission, clean routing APIs, examples, and documentation.
  * **[1.6] Hardened for LLM use cases**
      * By 1.6, Router EPP is hardened for LLM serving: the runtime-free deployment path is production-ready across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM rather than an early-adopter option.
  * **[1.6 - 1.7] Native-engine worker routing**

* **Sidecar**
  * **[1.5] Run unmodified upstream engine images**

      * Two contract options are under consideration: a vendor-neutral standardized gRPC spec (OpenEngine), or per-engine RPC adapters. Prototypes already exist for vLLM and SGLang.
  * **[1.5] Image input support for vLLM**
  * **[1.6] Hardened for LLM use cases**
      * By 1.6, the Sidecar is hardened for LLM serving across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM — closing the remaining gaps in disaggregated serving, metadata discovery, KV events and KV routing, deployment definitions, container and crate publishing, and end-to-end CI coverage.
  * **[1.6] Image input support for SGLang and TensorRT-LLM**
  * **[1.6 - 1.7] Video input support for SGLang and TensorRT-LLM**
  * **[1.7] Audio input support**
  * **[1.7+] Sidecar integration with the multimodal stack**

> **Stacked PR [3/3].** Base: #14177 (request classifier seam) ← #14176 (deadline queue ordering) ← `main`. This PR now carries only the dynamo-llm lifecycle integration and docs; the queue restructure and the classifier seam moved down the stack. Same final tree as the pre-split head `c732efa8fd`.

<!-- codex-pr-description:start -->
Adds an opt-in asynchronous request-classifier seam before Dynamo's router-owned policy scheduler, implementing the Classify → Order → Place flow proposed in DEP #13891. Dynamo keeps queueing, exact priority/deadline ordering, placement, cancellation, and terminal lifecycle ownership while plugins can defer admission and override validated Order inputs.

CLOSES: DYN-3885

Related to #13891

### How This Was Implemented

- Add an owned `ClassifyRequest` and independently pollable classifier future; the classifier mutex is held only while creating the future or delivering a short lifecycle callback.
- Validate classifier overrides, apply the plugin-set due time (caller-deadline clamping deferred until a caller deadline source exists), and send every admitted request through the existing policy-class and DRR queue before placement.
- Preserve exact `(strict_priority, due_at, policy_key, FIFO)` ordering with compact 64-byte queue entries and 40-byte worker-lane keys.
- Track only deadline-bearing entries in an ordered index so timer lookup is constant-time and full-queue expiry scans occur only when a deadline actually fires.
- Reuse cached-token eligibility, admission-counter, and lifecycle machinery instead of maintaining classifier-specific copies.
- Carry one RAII lifecycle through dispatch, retry, migration, response, and Drop so terminal cleanup and events remain exactly once.

<details>
<summary>Walkthrough</summary>

#### Mental model

The classifier controls when a request becomes eligible and may change only inputs consumed by Order. Dynamo validates the result, owns the queue and placement decision, and retains the terminal lifecycle backstop.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Ingress + lifecycle registration"] --> B["Async classifier future"]
    E["Ordered async lifecycle events"] --> F["Classifier-owned state"]
    F --> B
    B -->|"validated class, due time, cost"| C["Order: limits + exact priority + DRR"]
    C --> D["Place: existing filter + score + pick"]
    D --> G["Dispatch + response"]
    G --> E
```

#### State and ordering

Strict priority remains authoritative. Within one strict-priority tier, an earlier due time wins; the existing FCFS/WSPT/LCFS score and FIFO sequence break remaining ties. Caller-deadline clamping is deferred until the frontend supplies a deadline; the plugin-set due time is applied directly.

The DEP requires a classifier-set due time and earliest-due ordering; it does not prescribe the queue representation. The deadline-only `BTreeSet`, compact entry snapshot, flattened worker-lane key, and conditional actor timer are implementation choices that retain exact nanosecond ordering without imposing the prior 6–7% no-deadline hot-path regression.

#### Request lifecycle

Lifecycle ownership begins before classification. Selection records the worker before dispatch; successful dispatch, first response, normal completion, classifier failure, cancellation, retry exhaustion, and Drop converge on the same handle. A retry releases attempt-local state without terminating the logical request.

Lifecycle events are queued as owned values and delivered by a dedicated router task that awaits each `async fn on_event()` callback in order, so `Drop` can emit the terminal event from any thread by sending on the queue. Classification shutdown and caller expiry share one biased `select!`; cached overrides let retries avoid invoking the plugin again.

#### Boundaries and limitations

This does not change Filter/Score/Pick placement, add router-wide accounting for requests still pending in Classify, or invent the DEP's undefined predicted-deadline-miss policy. The cumulative received and due-time-passed counters are implemented.

This remains a draft. The current diff is `+2881/-198`; HTTP deadline-error mapping is still inconsistent across Anthropic, generic generate, SGLang initial-generate, and gRPC surfaces, and the classifier cost override still needs an actor-level immediate-capacity proof. DEP #13891 also remains in `dep:draft`.

The unmarked legacy description retained below this block is superseded by this walkthrough.

</details>

### Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-kv-router --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router` — 961 passed, 2 ignored
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib` — 2,316 passed, 3 ignored
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features recorder::tests::test_recorder_streams_events_to_file -- --exact` — 1 passed after one unrelated full-suite timing failure
- `git diff --check`

Criterion used 20 samples, a 1 s warm-up, a 3 s measurement window, and CPU affinity `6-7` against benchmark-baseline `main` commit `1df553558a`; the two later merged-main commits do not touch this benchmark or `policy_queue.rs`.

Both changes are inside Criterion's 3% noise threshold; the previous draft measured +5.97% and +6.90%.
<!-- codex-pr-description:end -->

---

### Summary

This adds an opt-in asynchronous request-classifier seam before Dynamo's router-owned policy-class scheduler, implementing the proposed Classify → Order → Place flow from DEP #13891. It matters because plugins can defer requests and set validated class, deadline, or DRR-cost inputs without owning queueing, placement, cancellation, or terminal lifecycle cleanup.

CLOSES: DYN-3885

Related to #13891

### How This Was Implemented

- Add an owned `ClassifyRequest` and `RequestClassifier`; `classify()` returns an independently pollable `'static` future so a pending request does not retain the classifier mutex.
- Route every valid classified request through one Order path, then drain it in the same actor turn when capacity is available; class limits, deadline checks, and DRR charging therefore apply consistently.
- Order requests by `(strict_priority, due_at, policy_key)` and apply classifier-supplied due times (caller-deadline clamping deferred until a caller deadline source exists).
- Carry one boxed RAII lifecycle from ingress through selection, dispatch, retry, migration, response, and Drop, with the selected worker recorded before dispatch and exactly one terminal event.
- Deliver lifecycle events through a dedicated task that awaits each `async fn on_event()` in order, publish cumulative received/deadline-expired counters, and preserve existing Filter/Score/Pick placement interfaces.
- Add scheduler, lifecycle, cancellation, deadline, query-only, retry, migration, and ThunderAgent-shaped pause/resume coverage plus the four priority-scheduling documentation updates.

<details>
<summary>Walkthrough</summary>

#### Mental model

The classifier controls when a request becomes eligible for scheduling and may change only the inputs consumed by Order. Dynamo retains the request, validates those inputs, applies its existing policy-class and DRR machinery, selects a worker through the existing Place interfaces, and owns terminal cleanup.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Ingress + RAII registration"] --> B["RequestClassifier future"]
    E["Ordered async lifecycle events"] --> F["Classifier-owned state"]
    F --> B
    B -->|"validated request metadata"| C["Order: class limit + strict priority + deadline + DRR"]
    C --> D["Place: existing filter + score + pick"]
    D --> G["Dispatch + response"]
    G --> E
```

#### State and ordering

Pending classifier futures run in request tasks rather than the scheduler actor. The plugin lock is held only while constructing the owned future or while the delivery task awaits one `on_event()` callback, so another request and event delivery can make progress while classification waits.

Every valid result enters `PolicyQueue`, including when a worker is idle. Strict priority is compared first; due time applies earliest-deadline-first ordering only within that strict-priority tier; the existing policy key and FIFO sequence break remaining ties. Cross-class fairness remains the existing DRR policy, charged with the validated per-request scheduling cost.

#### Request lifecycle

Lifecycle ownership begins before classification. Selection records the worker before dispatch; successful dispatch, first response, normal completion, classifier failure, cancellation, migration exhaustion, and Drop converge on the same boxed handle. A retry releases attempt-local worker state without terminating the logical request, while abort emits the terminal event exactly once.

Lifecycle events are owned values on an unbounded queue that is naturally bounded by live requests, drained by one router task that awaits each `on_event()` in lifecycle order. Terminal events therefore arrive asynchronously shortly after a request ends, a `Drop` on any thread only performs a queue send, and events still queued at router shutdown are dropped.

#### Boundaries and limitations

This does not change Filter/Score/Pick placement, add router-wide pending-token accounting, or implement the undefined predicted-deadline-miss policy. The DEP remains in `dep:draft`, so this PR records intentional deviations rather than amending or ratifying it.

This draft is not merge-ready. The rebased diff is `+2758/-164` versus the prior attempt's `+2342/-81`, so it does not yet meet the minimal-code target. The deadline error is currently rendered as HTTP 429 only by the OpenAI HTTP service; Anthropic, generic generate, SGLang initial generate, and gRPC still need matching handling. Deadline-aware queue wakeup currently scans all queued entries, the no-deadline admission benchmark regresses about 6–7%, and the classifier cost override still needs the required actor-level immediate-capacity test.

The three independent minimality gates were completed before publication. Gate 1 accepted changes reduced the diff by 26 net lines and Gate 3 by 5; Gate 2 fixes were applied, but its accepted/rejected line delta was not retained. Invariant-preservation review kept the `'static` future, ordered event delivery, boxed lifecycle, pre-dispatch worker record, separate retry release, and Drop terminal backstop.

</details>

### Deviations from DEP #13891

1. `on_event()` matches the DEP's `async fn` signature; `classify()` does not and **cannot**. An `async fn classify` future would borrow `&mut self` for its entire pending life, holding the router-wide classifier lock for the whole deferral and violating the DEP's own "one pending call MUST NOT block other requests, Order, or `on_event()` delivery". The property behind the DEP's signature — the plugin awaits, context-switches without blocking a thread, and needs no runtime of its own — holds for both methods. The DEP should record the property rather than the `classify` signature.
    - Events are delivered one at a time in lifecycle order by a dedicated router task; a pending `classify` never blocks delivery, terminal events arrive asynchronously shortly after a request ends, and events still queued at router shutdown are dropped.
    - Consequence for plugin authors, documented on the trait: because the classify future is `'static`, any state it touches must be owned or shared (`Arc`, channel sender, etc.) rather than borrowed from `self`, and the synchronous prologue of `classify` must return promptly.
2. The predicted-to-miss-due-time counter is not implemented because the DEP defines no predictor. The definable cumulative received and due-time-passed counters are implemented.
3. The lifecycle event type is named `ClassifyEvent`, not `QueueAdmissionEvent`.
4. Router-wide token accounting for requests pending in Classify is deferred; the draft DEP does not define that bound and this PR does not introduce one.

### Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-kv-router --lib -- -D warnings`
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router --lib` — 955 passed, 2 ignored
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib` — 2,254 passed, 3 ignored
- `cargo test -p dynamo-runtime deadline_exceeded_is_a_rejected_route_outcome --lib` — 1 passed
- `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD`

Three interleaved base/rebuild pairs were run for each Criterion case. These are regressions and remain an explicit draft blocker.

items.title: [BUG]: SGLang disaggregated requests with n > 1 hang after prefill completes

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Describe the Bug

An OpenAI-compatible chat completion request with `n > 1` hangs when served by an SGLang disaggregated prefill/decode deployment.

The frontend accepts and routes the request, the selected prefill worker finishes, and the selected decode worker receives the request. However, decode never emits a token or a terminal response. The client waits indefinitely unless it sets its own timeout.

The equivalent request with `n: 1` completes normally. This was reproduced repeatedly with `n: 2`; it does not appear to be a transient bootstrap registration race.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy Dynamo with the SGLang backend in a disaggregated 2-prefill/2-decode topology. The observed deployment used SGLang v0.5.18 and the Mooncake disaggregation transfer backend.
2. Start the standard Dynamo frontend with KV-aware routing.
3. Send a non-streaming request with `n: 2`:

```bash
curl --max-time 30 http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "<served-model>",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"}],
    "n": 2,
    "temperature": 0.1,
    "max_tokens": 64
  }'
```

4. Observe that the client times out without receiving any response bytes.
5. Repeat the request with `n: 1` and observe that it completes.

## Expected Behavior

The request should either:

- return two completed choices with indices 0 and 1; or
- be rejected promptly with a clear 4xx response if `n > 1` is not supported in SGLang disaggregated mode.

It should not remain pending indefinitely after prefill has completed.

## Actual Behavior

For a reproduced request:

- the decode worker received the request;
- the prefill worker received the same request, scheduled one sequence, and completed in about 207 ms;
- the decode worker produced no token and no completion event;
- the client timed out after 10 seconds with zero response bytes;
- longer client timeouts, including 30 seconds and approximately 243 seconds, showed the same behavior.

No `no such room` or bootstrap connection error was observed. This differs from #9388, which describes decode being released before the prefill room is registered.

The request flow also shows an `n`/handoff cardinality mismatch:

- the SGLang prefill handler forces the prefill sampling parameters to `n = 1` and yields one `bootstrap_room`;
- the decode handler forwards the original `n = 2` together with that single bootstrap room;
- SGLang parallel sampling expands the decode request into multiple independently identified requests and normalizes a scalar bootstrap room into multiple room values.

The selected prefill therefore completes one handoff while decode waits for all parallel samples.

## Environment

- Dynamo worker image source commit: `1e3478dfe09bdd305d7c58f412fda2dfe5bec7ed`
- SGLang: v0.5.18
- Deployment: Kubernetes, 2 prefill workers and 2 decode workers
- Frontend: `python3 -m dynamo.frontend --router-mode kv`
- Disaggregation transfer backend: Mooncake
- Request API: OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`
- Request mode reproduced: non-streaming, `n=2`, `temperature=0.1`

## Additional Context

There is an `n != 1` validation in the SGLang Python chat processor, but the deployed frontend path accepted and dispatched this request. Regardless of which frontend processor is selected, unsupported request cardinality should not reach a backend path that can wait indefinitely.

The issue was reproduced with a same-node prefill/decode pair as well as across repeated requests, so cross-node transport selection is not required to trigger it.

items.body:
# [CONTRIBUTION]: Add an agent-tree sibling placement benchmark

## Type of Change

New feature

## Problem Statement

Issue #11343 proposes parent-aware first-hop placement for subagent sessions, but the repository
does not currently have a controlled benchmark that distinguishes two different sources of wasted
prefill:

1. exact-prefix sibling requests first land on different Dynamo workers; or
2. siblings land on one worker but the engine still computes the same prefix concurrently.

Without backend worker attribution and cache-usage evidence, a placement change could be evaluated
against the wrong bottleneck. The existing router benchmarks do not produce the fan-out 2/4/8,
16k/32k exact-prefix matrix or the B0/B1/B2 controls needed for this distinction.

## Proposed Solution

Add a benchmark-only harness under `benchmarks/router/` that:

- generates one AIPerf 0.10.0 DAG row for fan-out 2/4/8, exact shared prefix 16k/32k, and burst or
  small jitter;
- uses a short control turn followed by SPAWN children, while verifying that the control prompt
  overlaps the children by less than one KV block and therefore cannot warm the measured prefix;
- runs unchanged against B0 default routing, B1 session-affinity co-location, and B2 existing
  KV-aware routing;
- parses AIPerf raw SSE records for Dynamo's prefill worker/DP-rank attribution, prompt tokens,
  cached tokens, computed prefill tokens, TTFT, and actual send skew;
- emits request-level CSV plus a Markdown decision (`KEEP`, `NEED_C1`, `NEED_C2`, or `STOP`);
- adds CPU-only unit tests for exact-prefix generation and decision attribution.

This proposal changes no runtime/router behavior and does not implement parent-aware placement or
engine-side leader prefill. It relates to #11343 by providing the measurement needed to decide
whether that placement work is warranted.

An implementation branch is available in the contributor fork for concrete scope review:
`JasperChan929/dynamo:bench/agent-tree-sibling-placement`. I will wait for maintainer approval of
this request before opening the pull request against `ai-dynamo/dynamo:main`.

Local validation completed so far:

- four focused unit tests pass;
- the generated Qwen3-0.6B 16k-prefix scenario has an exact 16,384-token sibling LCP and only one
  token of control/child overlap for a 16-token block size;
- the generated scenario loads successfully with the repository-pinned AIPerf 0.10.0 loader;
- all repository pre-commit hooks pass on the affected files.

## Estimated PR Size

XL (501-1000 lines)

## Files/Components Affected

- `benchmarks/router/agent_tree.py` (new generator, raw parser, and report writer)
- `benchmarks/router/agent_tree.md` (new execution and interpretation guide)
- `benchmarks/router/README.md` (benchmark index entry)
- `tests/benchmarks/test_agent_tree.py` (new CPU-only unit tests)

- [x] KV-aware routing and prefix-cache reuse (67.9%–77.2% prefix cache hit)

## Benchmark Results

| Recipe | GPUs | Concurrency | System tok/s | Per-GPU tok/s | TTFT P50 | TTFT P90 | ITL P50 | ITL P90 | Cache hit | Errors |
|--------|------|-------------|-------------|---------------|----------|----------|---------|---------|-----------|--------|
| Aggregated (1×TP4) | 4 | 24 | 1,830 | 457.4 | 329 ms | 1,851 ms | 9.7 ms | 15.1 ms | 67.9% | 130 (400) |
| Aggregated (2×TP4) | 8 | 24 | 2,474 | 309.3 | 339 ms | 1,306 ms | 7.8 ms | 12.8 ms | 73.1% | 130 (400) |
| **Aggregated (3×TP4)** | 12 | 24 | **2,857** | **238.1** | **325 ms** | **1,110 ms** | **6.9 ms** | 11.3 ms | 74.5% | 130 (400) |
| Disaggregated (1P1D) | 8 | 24 | 2,641 | 330.2 | 452 ms | 3,467 ms | 7.5 ms | 9.1 ms | 73.4% | 130 (400) |
| Disaggregated (2P1D) | 12 | 24 | 2,735 | 227.9 | 407 ms | 1,165 ms | 7.5 ms | 8.9 ms | 77.2% | 130 (400) |

- All 130 errors are 400 Bad Request (trace has requests exceeding 262K context limit) — 0 × 500, 0 × 503, 0 worker restarts.
- **8-GPU**: Disagg 1P1D is **+7% faster** than agg (2,641 vs 2,474 tok/s) but TTFT p90 is 2.7× worse (3,467 vs 1,306 ms) due to prefill queueing at `max-num-seqs=32`.
- **12-GPU**: Agg 3×TP4 is **+4.5% faster** than disagg 2P1D (2,857 vs 2,735 tok/s) and 20% better TTFT p50. Disagg wins on ITL p90 (8.9 vs 11.3 ms, -21%) and cache hit (77.2% vs 74.5%, +2.7pp).
- **2P1D fixes TTFT p90**: Adding a second prefill worker cuts TTFT p90 from 3,467 ms (1P1D) to 1,165 ms (-66%).
- KV transfer: ~18 GB/s avg via InfiniBand RDMA, 0 transfer failures.

See [BENCHMARK_REPORT.md](recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next/BENCHMARK_REPORT.md) for full details.

- **InfiniBand RDMA**: `UCX_TLS=rc_x,rc,cuda_copy,cuda_ipc` with `rdma/rdma_shared_device_a: 4` per worker. Achieves ~18 GB/s avg KV transfer (peak 42 GB/s) via GPUDirect RDMA (DMA-BUF). - **NCCL IB**: `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0`, `NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5`, `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5` for InfiniBand intra-pod TP communication.
- **Prefill `--max-num-seqs 32`**: reduced from 256 (used in agg) to avoid OOM on 260K-token prompts with only 4 GPUs. Decode keeps 256.

- **kv_role**: `kv_producer` (prefill) / `kv_consumer` (decode) — matches GLM-5.3-Flash pattern.

## Limitations

- Upstream image (ai-dynamo pip-installed, ~30s cold start overhead)
- No compile cache (ephemeral, ~5min cold start)
- Concurrency sweep not yet performed — C=24 is the single benchmarked point

## Follow-up work

- [x] Agg 8-GPU: smoke test + AIPerf benchmark

items.body:
## Overview:

`RoutingHost` records `record_prefill_start()` before every backend dispatch regardless of phase, so a decode-only request stamps a prefill-start timestamp at decode dispatch and `prefill_time_ms` then describes decode time as though it were prefill time. This makes the recording phase-aware.

## Details:

`prefill_start_time` is a write-once `OnceLock`, which is why the usual prefill-then-decode flow is unaffected: the prefill dispatch wins and the later decode call is a no-op. A decode-only request with a tracker has no earlier writer, so the decode dispatch becomes the first and only one.

The guard is placed in `RequestObservability::record_prefill_start()` rather than at the two call sites (`kv.rs:195`, `builtin.rs:336`) because both the KV and hosted-policy dispatch paths funnel through that struct. One change covers both, with no signature churn, no change to `phase_label`, and no change to worker selection, request admission, or routing accounting.

Reading the phase from the tracker is safe for the two callers that pass a hardcoded `RequestPhase::Prefill` (`routing_host.rs:531` and `kv.rs:269`): `prefill_router/mod.rs:378` calls `set_phase(RequestPhase::Prefill)` before dispatching and the tracker is a shared `Arc`, so `tracker.phase()` agrees with the caller there. Happy to switch to threading the phase through the call sites instead if you would rather not depend on that.

Resulting behaviour:

| Phase | prefill start recorded |
|---|---|
| `Prefill` | yes |
| `Aggregated` | yes |
| `Decode` | no |
| `Decode` after `Prefill` | keeps the timestamp prefill recorded (the later write is a no-op) |

## Where should the reviewer start?

`lib/llm/src/kv_router/routing_host/request_guard.rs` — the guard in `RequestObservability::record_prefill_start()`, then `mod prefill_start_tests` at the bottom of the file.

## Testing

Four tests, one per row of the table above. They build a real `RequestObservability` and call the production method rather than re-implementing the predicate; `RouterRequestMetrics` is constructed directly from plain prometheus types, so no runtime or registry is needed.

```

kv_router::routing_host                           45 passed
protocols::common::timing                         26 passed
cargo fmt --check / cargo clippy                   clean
```

items.title: refactor(router): unify conditional disagg routing host

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
1. Before and after

Before, `PrefillRouter` chose a decode worker itself. It looked up affinity, ran selection, and put the worker ID into request hints.

Then the decode `RoutingHost` read those hints. It did affinity work again, admitted the request, and sent it to the worker.

After, `PrefillRouter` asks the decode `RoutingHost` for a non-admitting route preview. The conditional policy decides local or remote from that preview; only a local decision asks the decode host to admit the previewed worker.

The remote path discards the preview and starts normal remote prefill immediately.

2. Was it useful?

Yes. It removes duplicate worker-selection work and the internal selected-worker request hint.

It also moves the topology choice before decode admission, so remote prefill is not delayed by decode queueing.

This change does not promise a throughput increase. Its value is correct ownership, less duplicate code, safer cancellation, and unbiased routing metrics.

3. Do prefill and decode have their own routing hosts?

Yes.

- The prefill side has a `RoutingHost` for the remote prefill worker set.
- The decode side has one `RoutingHost` for the decode worker set.

<!-- codex-pr-description:start -->
Conditional disaggregation now previews a decode route without admitting it, then admits the previewed worker only when topology selects local prefill plus decode. This lets remote prefill start without waiting for decode capacity, keeps selection and admission host-owned, and avoids speculative routing metric samples.

### How This Was Implemented

- Add a host-owned `RoutePreview` with decode cache, load, and locality signals but no queue entry, reservation, or affinity lease.
- Evaluate `ConditionalDisaggPolicy` from that preview; discard it for remote prefill, or have `RoutingHost` admit the same worker for local dispatch.
- Keep the previewed worker inside `RoutingHost`; it is never written into caller-owned routing hints.
- Preserve cancellation as terminal, treat only non-cancellation prefill-load probe failures as unavailable data, and reject reuse with a different decode host.
- Remove the ignored `PrefillRouter::new` decode-router argument and the obsolete direct admitted-plan path.

<details>
<summary>Walkthrough</summary>

#### Route lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as PrefillRouter
    participant H as Decode RoutingHost
    participant K as KV selector and scheduler
    participant E as Decode engine

    P->>H: preview_kv_route(request)
    H->>K: query selection only
    K-->>H: RoutePreview(signals, worker)
    H-->>P: preview
    alt local prefill plus decode
        P->>H: plan_kv_route_from_preview(request, preview)
        H->>K: acquire affinity and admit previewed worker
        H->>E: dispatch admitted route
    else remote prefill
        P->>P: discard preview and start normal remote prefill
    end
```

The preview is a point-in-time policy input, not a reservation. A local decision may wait in normal decode admission, but that happens after the policy has committed to local execution; a remote decision never waits on decode capacity.

#### Ownership and failure paths

`RoutingHost` builds both the preview and the admitted route, including explicit-target and affinity conflict validation. The prefill router owns only topology. A cancellation from previewing, probing, or admitting returns immediately; a non-cancellation prefill-load probe error becomes an unavailable policy fact.

#### Boundaries

The previewed worker is deliberately pinned only within the host when local execution is chosen, keeping target-specific policy facts aligned with dispatch without leaking an internal worker choice through request hints. The preview is still a point-in-time assessment: if local admission cannot proceed, normal routing error behavior applies.

</details>

### Validation

- `cargo fmt --all`
- `cargo check -p dynamo-llm --lib --message-format=short`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib route_preview --quiet` (2 passed)
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib route_plan --quiet` (3 passed)
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib conditional_disagg --quiet` (2 passed)
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib --quiet` (2,440 passed, 5 ignored)
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-llm --lib -- -D warnings`

## Overview:

Adds a frontend-authoritative Prometheus metric indicating whether Dynamo can currently route requests for a model. This gives external dispatchers a reliable capacity signal so they can preserve queued work when no serving capacity is ready and resume dispatch as soon as the first complete serving unit becomes routable.

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Summary

`ModelRuntimeConfig::kv_event_source_mode` states its own contract:

> Accepted values are `framework_v1` and `state_agent_v2`. Missing means the legacy Worker-only source. Unknown explicit values must disable KV-aware routing rather than falling back within the same worker lifecycle.

Two consumers read that field and disagreed on what satisfies it:

| Site | Test | Unrecognized mode |
|------|------|-------------------|
| `state_agent.rs` `source_mode_suppressed_workers` | allowlist `None \| Some("framework_v1")` | suppressed (correct) |
| `kv_router.rs` `transfer_hint_for_selection` | denylist `!= Some("state_agent_v2")` | **still eligible** |

So a worker advertising a mode this router does not recognize -- a newer engine rolled out ahead of the router, or a typo in the field -- gets suppressed from the state-agent indexer while still being picked as a KV transfer hint source. The router hands a client the `source_control_endpoint` of a worker whose KV state it has deliberately stopped tracking, and nothing logs it.

The fix routes both consumers through one predicate defined next to the field, so the contract has a single definition rather than two that can drift. That also deletes the duplicated `matches!` in `state_agent.rs`.

This replaces the original version of this PR. That one predated #13134, which reshaped this code into the typed KV hint contract and removed `router_hint_metadata_for_dp_rank` entirely; the denylist above is where the same defect now lives, so the fix was rewritten against current `main` rather than rebased.

## Validation

Rebased onto `61c37bc33c`. `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib`: **2424 passed, 0 failed, 3 ignored**. `cargo clippy -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib` clean on the touched files (the one remaining warning is pre-existing in `lib/mocker/src/common/utils.rs:114`).

The new test fails on the unfixed code. Reverting only the one-line predicate swap at the fix site and keeping the test:

```
test kv_router::tests::kv_transfer_ignores_worker_source_with_unrecognized_event_source_mode ... FAILED

assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Some(KvSourceLocationsPayload { source_control_endpoint: "tcp://stale-worker-endpoint:23280", ... })
 right: Some(KvSourceLocationsPayload { source_control_endpoint: "tcp://persistent-owner:23280", ... })
```

That is the bug stated as output: the worker with the unrecognized mode wins the hint over the eligible persistent owner. The test mirrors the existing `kv_transfer_resolves_persistent_owner_without_state_agent_fallback` and changes one literal, so it covers the unrecognized-mode case beside the known-mode case it was modeled on.

GPU, multi-node, and live-engine paths were not exercised; this is a CPU-only unit-level change.

items.title: [FEATURE]: Standalone epp: auto-calibrate `DYN_KV_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE` from kv events

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
### Feature request

Let the standalone epp learn the kv event block size by itself instead of requiring the exact value in `DYN_KV_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE`. The `BlockStored` events already carry the block size so the epp could simply adopt the main-attention block size from the first event it receives, and keep the env var as an explicit override. It would also make the standalone epp + gaie combo truly self-contained and more modular.

### Describe the problem you're encountering

The standalone epp (gaie with vanilla vllm) needs `DYN_KV_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE` to exactly match the engine block size. The thing is that for hybrid mamba models vllm re aligns the attention block size at engine boot:

`Setting attention block size to 2096 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size.`

so the real value is only knowable from a running engine, and it varies per model. When the configured value doesn't match, the router drops every single event:

`WARN zmq_wire::convert: Block not published. Block size must be 16 tokens to be published. Block size is: 2096`

and kv-aware routing silently degrades to load-only. This is the standalone sibling of #9376 -> the dynamo vllm worker solves it by asking the engine directly (`get_kv_cache_group_metadata`), but the standalone epp has no engine handle.

### Describe alternatives you've tried

- static per model values read from the engine boot logs. It works but it's fragile: the value shifts with vllm versions, attention backend and cache dtype changes, and nothing tells you when it becomes wrong
- patching our custom vllm image to expose the engine metadata over http, like the dynamo worker does in-process, and filling DYN_KV_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE from it at deploy time

items.title: DEP: Hard and soft session affinity in the router pipeline

labels.name: router
labels.description: Relates to routing, KV-aware routing, etc.

items.body:
## Summary

Define hard and soft session affinity as two interpretations of the same mode-agnostic session binding. Hard affinity converts a live binding into an exact routing constraint. Soft affinity exposes the binding as a policy-visible preference, preserves the normal candidate pipeline, and changes the binding only after a successful dispatch. Hard remains the default for compatibility.

This proposal builds on the unified `RoutingHost` lifecycle and the pluggable worker-selection interfaces. It does not introduce another router mode or a second routing pipeline.

## Motivation

Today, a session binding is effectively hard: a live binding becomes an exact worker or worker/rank target. That preserves locality, but it cannot express migratable agentic sessions whose placement policy may move them because of load, eligibility, or application-specific signals.

Treating every binding as soft would weaken explicit routing and existing sticky-session behavior. Treating soft affinity as a special bypass would also skip the filter/score/pick extension point that should own policy decisions. The router needs a precise distinction between:

- an exact target that policies cannot replace; and
- a current affinity target that policies may retain or replace.

The distinction should not leak into the affinity coordinator. The coordinator owns binding lifecycle and convergence; `RoutingHost` owns how a request interprets a binding.

## Proposal

### Configuration and terms

Add a session-affinity mode with `hard` as the default:

```text
--router-session-affinity-mode hard|soft
```

The mode is meaningful only when session affinity is enabled. `x-dynamo-session-id` supplies a session lookup key; it is not an explicit worker target. Existing phase-specific worker and DP-rank targeting fields remain strict in both modes.

Use two request-level concepts:

```rust
pinned_target: Option<RouteTarget>   // exact constraint
affinity_target: Option<RouteTarget> // policy-visible preference
```

An explicit request target always becomes `pinned_target`. A stored session binding becomes `pinned_target` in hard mode and `affinity_target` in soft mode. A conflicting explicit target for an existing live binding is rejected rather than silently mutating the session.

### Selection matrix

| Selection policy | Hard session binding | Soft session binding |
|---|---|---|
| Hosted built-ins: round-robin, random, power-of-two-choices, least-loaded, device-aware | Validate and dispatch the exact target through the existing target fast path | If the affinity target is selectable, retain it; otherwise run the normal built-in selector |
| Default KV selector | Validate the exact worker/rank and use the existing pinned-target path | Exact-check the affinity target. If eligible, narrow the candidate set to that worker/rank and naturally run the existing score/pick path over the singleton. If ineligible, run normal KV selection over all eligible candidates |
| Custom filter/score/pick policy | The target is a hard eligibility constraint, so the custom pipeline sees at most the pinned candidate and cannot choose another target | The custom pipeline receives the normal candidate set and can inspect `WorkerSelectionContext::affinity_target()` to retain, penalize, filter, or ignore the current binding |
| Direct | Preserve exact-target semantics; Direct has no alternate selector and therefore gains no implicit soft fallback | Same |

For a worker-only target, exact narrowing looks up that worker directly and exposes only its valid DP ranks. For a worker/rank target, it exposes exactly one candidate row. A healthy hard binding uses exact dispatch. A healthy default soft KV binding materializes only the target worker or worker/rank before normal score/pick; prompt-index lookup cost is unchanged.

### Request flow

```text
request
  -> extract session_id and explicit_target
  -> acquire binding operation from AffinityCoordinator
  -> RoutingHost resolves pinned_target / affinity_target
  -> eligibility and policy selection
  -> admission and dispatch
  -> commit the actual dispatched target
  -> retain the affinity lease through the response stream
```

The coordinator remains mode-agnostic:

```rust
let operation = coordinator.acquire(session_id).await?;
let targets = resolve_targets(explicit_target, operation.target(), affinity_mode)?;
let selected = select(request, targets).await?;
let stream = dispatch(selected).await?;
operation.commit(actual_dispatched_target)?.track(stream)
```

`RoutingHost` owns `RoutingLoadContext`, `Option<AffinityCoordinator>`, and `SessionAffinityMode` as sibling fields. No additional routing-context wrapper is required.

### Hard-affinity failure behavior

Hard affinity must not silently become soft whenever its target is inconvenient.

- A definitively removed worker or invalidated DP rank invalidates the observed binding and fails the current exact dispatch. The next request performs normal selection and binds its successful target.
- Overload, request constraints, custom-filter rejection, admission rejection, cancellation, or transient dispatch/backend errors never invalidate the binding. Request handling otherwise follows the existing exact-target path for that policy; for example, a KV admission check may reject an overloaded pin.
- Invalidation is conditional on the observed binding generation so stale requests cannot delete a newer binding.

### Soft rebinding

Soft selection never mutates the binding before dispatch succeeds.

- Dispatch to the current target refreshes the binding.
- Successful dispatch to another target performs a compare-and-swap rebind against the observed binding version.
- Failed alternate dispatch preserves the old binding.
- If concurrent migrations race, the first successful CAS wins. Losing requests may still complete successfully but do not overwrite the winner.
- Cancellation does not invalidate or migrate a binding.
- Releasing a lease from an older generation cannot refresh or overwrite a newer binding.

Query-only selection remains read-only: it does not initialize, refresh, or rebind a session.

### Coordinator and replica updates

Keep local generation and replicated ordering separate:

- A local binding generation prevents ABA when an entry is removed and recreated.
- Replicated updates carry an ordered version such as `(sequence, writer_id)`.
- Replicas accept only newer updates, including conflicting targets.
- Router replicas in one deployment use the same update schema; this intracomponent protocol does not add a mixed-version compatibility shim.

The coordinator continues to own TTL, active leases, initialization serialization, capacity limits, and replica publication. It does not depend on load state and does not know whether the caller is using hard or soft affinity.

This remains a best-effort, TTL-scoped affinity plane rather than a durable consensus store.

### Performance requirements

- A request without a session ID follows the existing routing path after one optional branch.
- Hard target validation uses direct worker lookup and does not scan all workers.
- A healthy default soft KV target uses direct lookup, materializes only that worker or worker/rank, and runs the existing score/pick path over that narrowed candidate set.
- Custom soft policies retain the existing full candidate cost because policy code is allowed to choose another target.
- Session handling must not bypass admission, load accounting, request guards, dispatch monitoring, or stream cleanup.

### Validation

Focused tests should cover:

- hard and soft behavior for round-robin, random, power-of-two-choices, least-loaded, device-aware, default KV, and custom policies;
- worker-only and worker/rank bindings;
- dead targets versus overload, constraints, filter rejection, cancellation, and transient dispatch failure;
- first-request initialization and concurrent waiters;
- successful soft rebind, failed alternate dispatch, CAS races, ABA prevention, and stale lease release;
- query-only behavior;
- ordered replica conflicts and schema-consistent replica updates;
- multiple frontend/router replicas with many mock workers;
- a no-session and affinity-hit performance comparison.

## Alternate Solutions

### Treat every session binding as hard

This preserves current behavior but prevents policy-controlled migration for agentic sessions.

### Treat every session binding as soft

This weakens existing sticky-session behavior and explicit target guarantees. Hard remains the compatibility default.

### Encode hard or soft in replicated binding state

Rejected. A binding is only session-to-target state. Interpretation belongs to the local routing host, allowing the same replicated state to be consumed under either policy.

### Bypass selection for all soft affinity hits

Rejected for custom policies because it prevents filters, scorers, and pickers from exercising their intended authority. The default KV implementation may narrow to an eligible affinity target because its defined behavior is to retain that target.

### Introduce another shared routing-context wrapper

Rejected. `RoutingHost` already owns the lifecycle and can retain load state, affinity state, and mode directly. A wrapper would add indirection without enforcing a new invariant.

## Requirements

- Hard is the default mode and preserves existing explicit-target behavior.
- Hard and soft use one session binding representation and one coordinator.
- Explicit request targets are always strict.
- Hard bindings constrain selection; soft bindings are policy-visible preferences.
- Default KV soft affinity narrows to an eligible exact target before normal score/pick and falls back to the full candidate set when ineligible.
- Custom soft policies receive `affinity_target` without automatic candidate narrowing.
- Binding creation and migration occur only after successful dispatch.
- Dead-binding invalidation and soft rebinding use generation-checked mutation.
- Replica conflict resolution is ordered and deterministic.
- Existing routing admission, accounting, cancellation, and stream lifecycle remain intact.
- The no-session hot path and exact-target paths do not gain an all-worker scan.

## References

- #10883 — session affinity across typed paths and WorkerSets
- #11035 — cross-replica affinity divergence
- #12998 — unified LLM routing strategy pipeline
- #13163 — earlier hard/soft session-affinity implementation
- #13861 — routing-context load ownership used as the implementation base
